INTRODUCTION 1 FAUST?! A) Personal relationship between Fausto and Agustín

Judging by his Confessions, the name of Faustus reached Augustine's ears shortly after entering the sect. Unable to respond to the serious questions that the young man posed, the African leaders delayed him, referring him to the arrival of Fausto. Thus, for almost nine years, Augustine waited for him with lively desire (Conf. V 6,10). Propaganda had presented him as a man very learned in all kinds of sciences and, above all, educated in the liberal arts. A simple dialogue with him would be enough, they told him, so that, with the utmost ease, he could clarify whatever was obscure (Conf. V 6,10). Perhaps this is the only explanation why the young man waited so long. From him he awaited the solution to the doubts that arose after reading the philosophical and scientific books (Conf. V 3,3).

Since there is no evil that lasts a hundred years, the Manichaean finally arrived. For the moment, and not without disappointment, Agustín had to content himself with listening to him as one of the listeners, without being able to engage in the vaunted direct dialogue with him. Or what is the same, without being able to explain their difficulties. Finally he succeeded and, in the company of his friends, he was able to chat with him as he liked, until he even managed to have him as a student (Conf. V 7,13).
The judgment he gives about him does not respond to what was the opinion among the Manichaeans. He did not find him as wise as they said nor with sufficient preparation to solve the issues.

On a religious level, he calls it the “devil's snare” and notes that the movement of his heart did not mark the direction towards God (1b.). At this same level, and as far as he was concerned personally, the effect it had on him was considerable. Having lost hope that he or other doctors would solve his difficulties, he saw how all his interest in the writings of Manés and his desire to progress in the sect collapsed (Conf. V 7,12-13). So that the one who had been a death snare for others, without knowing it or wanting it, had begun to loosen the one that held him tied to him (1b.).

LI. Faust 5 B) The character

But who was this Faust? We know the specific information about him mainly from the work Contra Faustum. He was an African, born around 340 according to the opinion of Monceaux?, in Milevi (modern Mila, in Algeria), a town located in the province of Numidia (11; V 5). His family was poor (V 5), still pagan according to their own confession (1X 1; XII 1; XV 1; XIX 1.5). Regarding his intellectual formation, we already made reference to the data provided by Agustín in Confessiomes, which we will later complete with those of Contra Faustum, when talking about this work.

He claims to have left father and mother, wife and children (V 1; cf. Mt 19:29), so it is conceivable that he was married. Although, with respect to his wife and children, it is also possible to interpret that he left them as he renounced marriage. The reason for such behavior was none other than his entry into the Manichean religion. We do not know the process that led to that decision and the date of it. Without a doubt he went directly from paganism to Manichaeism. However, in some text he hints at a certain seduction of Judaism at a certain moment (XIX 5). As a certain date we have the year 383 in which he arrived in Carthage, already as a Manichaean bishop, and Augustine's meeting with him took place (Conf. V 3,3). Without forgetting the fact, already mentioned, from Augustine himself according to which he eagerly awaited his arrival during the almost nine years in which he was a Manichean listener. It was due to the fame he enjoyed among the members of the sect that, from his first difficulties, the other catechists had referred him to him (Conf. V 6,10). This would place us around 370 at least, leaving a margin of time for him to achieve celebrity.

He arrived in Carthage, already as bishop (Corf. V 3,3), where Augustine had the opportunity to come into contact with him. We already know the impression it left on him. It is not known for sure where it came from. Perhaps from Rome, where it is known that he lived for some time, next to a certain Constantius (V 5), about whom Augustine also informs us in another work *. There it caused a schism, when the Matarians separated, scandalized by the simple life they led (V 5; De haeres. 46,10).
Denounced, along with other coreligionists, by the Catholics, he had to appear before the judge. Before him he was convicted

II. The work of Faust 7 and three of these chapters, of varying length *. At least those are the ones that Augustine has refuted, without us being allowed to know for sure if he has refuted the entire work. Or what is the same, if the entire work came into his hands, since he explicitly claims to have refuted all the false accusations contained in them (XXXIII 9) ".

But what is a capitulum? From the outset, the idea of “chapters” of Scripture in our modern meaning must be excluded *. The division of it into chapters and verses is much later than the patristic era. However, the term always refers to a text of Scripture, of unequal length, that is the subject of a controversy *. That is, it is not brought up to exegete it, but to use it as a weapon in a dispute. "The capitulum constitutes the basis and argument of the disputatio and Augustine can speak of the capitula of Faust whose slander he has refuted. The term designates in its entirety a disputatio on a scriptural text as well as the dogmatic or moral teaching that arises from said exegesis" **. In reality, the capitula are thematic units in which Faust concentrates the divergences between Manichean and Catholic doctrine.

Whether Augustine transmitted all of the chapters or not, there is no doubt that the order that he has preserved for us is not the original of Faust. Disorder in the presentation of the themes and internal inconsistencies prove it. An example: Faustus announces in XXXII 6 that he will later examine whether the prophets have announced Christ, a point that he does not mention again and that, however, was previously considered.

IL. The work of Faust 9 private, with the Catholics (I 2). It is addressed, therefore, to the Manichaeans themselves, to the “dearest brothers” (zb.). It is “a manual for the perfect Manichaean debater.” He presents it as a work of defense, a brief and concise response to the devious and cunning propositions of his opponents (1b.). In fact, it always begins by presenting a question, which implies an objection, fictitious or real, put into the mouth of a Catholic, which he then refutes. What happens is that Fausto seems well convinced that the best defense is a good attack. Augustine had already detected this, although referring to the Manichaeans in general: “I saw that their eloquence was richer and more refined when it came to refuting the errors of others than secure and firm in the exposition of their own doctrines” (De utilitate credendi 1,2). In fact, his defense immediately turns into merciless harassment of the opponent. Sometimes the fictitious dialogue is prolonged with several interventions by each party.'” One perceives someone very trained in hand-to-hand debate.

Fausto's writing is an invaluable document for us. First because of what he himself says, both about his own and his opponents, the Catholics, and then because of what he encouraged Augustine to say. Testimony at the same time of the doctrine that it combats and that it defends. It is a direct testimony, in its literal tenor, without any complications other than those that may arise from the transmission of the text, since there can be no doubt about Agustín's intellectual honesty. Modern findings have confirmed that the Manichaean bishop is a reliable testimony of Manichaeism itself, not only of an alleged African Manichaeism with its own features, substantively different from those of other geographical environments.

But anyone expecting a systematic presentation of the sect's doctrinal heritage will be disappointed, particularly with regard to the description of the myth. We cannot forget the character of the work, nor what Agustín stated and has remembered little: that they are more skilled in attacking the opponent's positions than in defending their own. The debater, if he is skillful and cautious like Faustus, knows how to choose the terrain and enters only where he sees an easy way out (Conf V 7,12). If Augustine is forced by the writing of Faust, which he refutes, to touch on certain topics, that is not the case with Faust. Having taken the initiative, he has chosen the combat field that best suits him.
In the prologue the Manichean bishop pays just tribute to the founder of the sect, Manés “our father”, and to whom

Adeimantus possibly introduced this religion in Africa, accompanying him with a good compliment: after that, the only one that deserves to be studied. Its wheel is set in the writing itself (I 2). After this very “Manichean” prologue, as if to give group consciousness, they almost disappear from the scene; With the exception of a few and very brief references to Manes, as his teacher (XIX 5), as the theologian (XX 3) and as the Paraclete (XXXII 6), the work becomes "Christian" in the argument and in the themes. On the one hand, the writings of either father of the sect are not used with evidentiary value. Only once and in a generic way does it allude to the fact that the "Fathers" have already shown that the prophets did not predict anything about Christ (XX 1) has no one to force him to resort to them, as happened to Fortunatus and Felix. On the other hand, he avoids the specific themes of the Manichean myth, which have no parallel in Christian teaching. It was a wise tactic, recommended by experience. done if he himself had directly provided him with the opportunity!

Manichaeans and Catholics fought for Christian ownership and reality (12). Faust claims the original character of his sect, denying that it is a schism from paganism, Judaism, or the Catholic Church (XX 4). Rather, it is Judaism and the Catholic Church that are a schism of paganism, which, with Manichaeism, are the original religions? The mutual accusation of paganism necessarily led to defending one's own Christian character. But defining the Christian character could only be done from the previous definition of the figure of Christ, which came to occupy a predominant place in the Manicheo-Catholic debate 2. At the same time, defining his figure could only be done from the argument of authority (XXVII 1), which required as a precondition delimiting the terrain within which such argumentation was valid. Finally, other doctrinal derivations emerged from the Christological discussion that fueled the controversy.

More than a theologian, Faustus is an exegete. Therefore, the greatest wealth of information it offers us refers to the previous aspect to which we have alluded. Your writing reaffirms something for us.

IL. The work of Faustus 11 already known from other sources: the exclusion of the Old Testament and the nuanced and mutilated acceptance of the New, both of the gospels and of the Apostle. To defend the teaching of his sect, the Manichaean bishop virulently attacks Catholic Scripture in its extension and in its very interpretation. It is not only that they reject the Old Testament en bloc, or that they mutilate the New, - on the other hand, without clearly and objectively establishing its material limits -, they also did not always agree in the interpretation of the relatively little that they had left in common. Formally, Catholics and Manichaeans accepted Scripture as a valid criterion of truth. They also saw in the Paraclete, who, according to Jn 14:26, would teach all things, the prior criterion that authenticates it. But they disagreed when identifying him. For the Manichaeans, this Paraclete is not the one whose coming is narrated in the Acts of the Apostles and whose teaching is continued through the apostolic succession in the various churches, but rather he appears in the person of the founder of their religion, Manes. He, then, or rather his teaching, whose central dogma is dualism, is the criterion according to which the Scriptures will be evaluated (XXXI 7). Hence the prior examination to which they are subjected, which we will see later. The richness of Faust lies not only in informing us of the data, but above all in providing, with abundance and detail, the concrete reasoning and the Manichaean procedure regarding Catholic Scripture. The particular interconnection between dogma, morality and exegesis of Scripture is also obvious, the former being the criterion for the latter and not the other way around. In effect, all discussion about the authenticity and interpretation of a biblical text is done in the shadows and from the criterion of a point of a dogmatic or moral nature, explicit or not.

The figure of Christ was, we said, a central point in the debate. In this regard, the information that Faust gives us is not as much as the modern historian of religions would like, but it is not little. In his pen we see the so-called historical Jesus, accepted by the Catholic Church, being dehistoricized. Under the mantle of Docetism, proclaimed loudly, her earthly birth of a woman and everything that is a consequence of it disappears: the stories of childhood, baptism, temptation in the desert, and passion, crucifixion, death and scars become pure appearance. Passion and crucifixion that, however, do not disappear from the language of the sect, but to acquire a meaning of a mystical nature. Indeed, within the silence that generally surrounds the features of the myth, the Manichaean bishop does not overlook the other figures typical of the sect:

12 Introduction the suffering Jesus (lesus patibilis) and the Jesus-Light (XIV 1). And, in connection with Jesus, there is a reference to his Trinity (XX 2), to his “Eucharist” (XX 2), to his creative function of the new man, given that the old man is not the work of God (XXIV 1) and to his worship of the sun and the moon (XX 1).

As it constitutes the core of the system, the mention of radical dualism could not be missing, which he contrasts with the opinion of monarchy (XX 3.4), of the double principle of good and evil (XXI 1) and, ultimately, the discussion on the uniqueness (XXI 1) and limited character of God (XXV 1). Finally, indirectly, Fausto informs us about aspects of dietary and sexual morality. Little, very little, is what he lets fall on the organization of the sect, without once mentioning by name either the listeners or the chosen ones. Just a mention of the “priestly class” (XXX 1).

Fausto's personality is attractive to anyone who approaches him. But not always pleasant." What causes the most emotional distance from him is undoubtedly his arrogance, the image he tries to give of himself. "Humility is not exactly his strong point." In fact, he surprises by presenting himself as the perfect fulfiller of the gospel, specifically of the beatitudes. This fulfillment turns him into proof that he accepts the gospel, in the face of the adversary's insinuating question (V 1). He has chosen the hardest part of it (V 2). He presumes his sincerity, of saying what he feels (VI DE of a spiritual man par excellence, who does not need to beg for miserable inheritances, which even if they were free would mortify him (IV 1); of profound piety regarding Christ, which prevents him from recognizing Moses (XIV 1); of a purely spiritual cult (XX 3); of preferring the use of reason to a headless happiness (XVI 8).

On the other hand, he simulates humility by showing himself willing to be taught: “unless your wisdom teaches me otherwise” (IV 1). He wants to show that he is not stubborn; that he is willing to surrender, as long as the Catholic is able to show him what he demands of him (III 1). At the same time, he shows confidence in himself and in his reasoning. On the one hand, he proclaims to be willing not to shy away from any debate, since he has an abundance of answers (II 1); On the other hand, he renounces further possibilities of reply, because he believes that a first one is enough (XXXIII 3; XXI 2). Try to present yourself as a man

11. The work of Faust 13 broad views that I wish not only Moses, but all the Jewish and Gentile prophets had written about Jesus (XVI 10).

Beyond how he sees himself or how he wants to be seen, the reader cannot help but notice other more objective data. The first, who speaks and writes from a personal and direct documentation. All of his writing testifies to his extensive and deep knowledge of Scripture, both the Old and New Testaments. He also knows the interpretation of both by the Catholic Church 2. He is aware of the ascetic practices of his faithful (XXX 2-6). Although on some occasions he claims not to know whether a certain point of view satisfies the Catholic faith (XXI 2), he is also up to date with respect to its content. We can summarize the Augustinian refutation in these lines of action: 1) Discreditation of the adversary; 2) Rational-based argumentation. 3) Argument from authority; 4) Argument from the evidence; 5) Ad hominem argument.

2. RATIONAL BASIS ARGUMENTATION

In his writing Faustus accused Catholics of condemning reason in men (XVIII 3). As might be expected, Augustine explicitly denies this (XVIII 7). But it could be argued that the best refutation of what the Manichaean bishop stated is Augustine's own reply writing. We are not referring only to its rational use of the various types of argumentation it uses. Indeed, the preponderance of biblical evidence does not exclude its recourse to specifically rational argumentation.

This is the case, for example, when he refutes the accusation that Catholics are in error because they are closer to pagans than the Manichaeans. The Saint supports his argument in a long exposition about the various differentiating criteria on which classifications are usually established (XX 10).

The argument from reason gives particular weight in the discussion on the dualism of principles and their nature (XXI 14). Logic should lead the Manichaeans to affirm not one good and one bad principle, but two good principles, although one better than the other (XXI 16).
His reflections on sin, eternal law and natural order (XXII 27ff) are also placed in the rational realm.

When in the twenty-sixth book the Manichean bishop resorts to logic to refute the positions of the Catholics, Augustine also meets him with rational arguments, stopping at what is or is not in accordance with nature and in reflections on the omnipotence of God (XXVI 5-6).

Augustine's argument is summarized in the following ideas: The patriarchs and prophets, even as the Manichaeans imagine them, are better than their God (XXII 12.22.23.98; XXXIII 4). Even his worshipers are better than him, because at least they exist (XXII 98). This, in effect, is nothing more than a false fiction and an empty thought (XXIT 98). The statement does not stop there: the vices of the patriarchs are to be put before the virtues that they presume in their chosen ones (XXII 23).

The same can be said of other texts. Since they consider human birth to be unworthy of Christ, he puts before their eyes what they believe about their First Man (11 2). As they deny the story of the wise men, because it would be subjecting Christ to the stars, he argues with them with his belief that Christ is linked to the stars (11 5). They who despise the visible land of the Canaanites, thus describe the Land of light (IV 2). Faustus claims not to desire other people's goods, but he must not have learned it from his God; But why did he build new centuries on the land of darkness, which did not exist before? (X 3). Due to his presumption of possessing arguments so powerful that they exclude the need for witnesses, he presents them with questions regarding the three periods of the myth for which they have no answer (XIII 6). IV. THE REPLICA TO THE REPLICA

We know that Faust's writing made an impact on Catholic spirits. Proof of this is the same Augustinian reply, at the request of other brothers. But we ignore the reaction that this provoked in the Manichaeans. Unfortunately for us, Faustus, having died earlier, did not have the opportunity to reply to Augustine. And no other cult member, that we know of, did. In the event that this was the case, we are not in a position to affirm whether it was due to a lack of strength to confront the Catholic bishop, the explicit desire not to give him free publicity or because they considered it unnecessary. But it is very likely that, internally, Augustinian's work was not left without some type of replica. The hierarchs would have to give their response to reassure the listeners, convincing them that the criticisms were not pertinent (cf. Comf. V 11, 21). And not out of pure polemical desire, but because that was his personal conviction.

If Faustus had been comfortable with Catholic positions, Augustine was not far behind. The Manichean bishop wrote for his coreligionists, the Catholic fundamentally for his own as well. And the arguments that work at home don't always work on the street. Certain reasonings can serve very well to prevent a Catholic from joining the Manichean ranks, but they will hardly make a convinced Manichean join or return to the Catholic Church. As we already indicated, it is the first that interests Agustín the most.

The argument of authority did not affect them either. Augustine reduced everything to the personal whim of the Manichaeans, to a matter of pure “carnal” sensitivity, something completely subjective. They knew that this was not the case, that they had an objective criterion, which were the writings of Manés, from which they judged what theoretically had to unite Catholics and Manichaeans: the Scripture.

The authentic interpretation, from the Catholic point of view, of the Old Testament occupies many pages of Augustinian writing. Faust knew how to extract sharp weapons against Catholic beliefs from the anthropomorphisms and moral behavior of patriarchs and prophets. Catholics found an easy way out by resorting to allegorical-typological interpretation. The Manichaeans opt for the attack by reducing any spiritual interpretation to the activity of an overly active imagination or to a pure waste of ingenuity (XII 37). The support that Augustine obtains from the Apostle (1 Cor 10:11), accepting that the text is authentic, does not mean anything in terms of the specific meanings attributed to the texts. The specific criterion, as a rule, is not dictated by the Apostle, but by the tradition of the Catholic Church. Therefore, this argument left the Manichean cold, while at the same time it could strengthen the Catholic.

The same can be said of any argument supported by the authority of Scripture. The Saint argues from our books: “The authority of our books is adverse to you” (XII 5). From here on, the Manichaeans did not feel addressed, although the Catholics saw the doctrine presented to them by their pastors confirmed.

There are undoubtedly fewer pages that the bishop of Hippo dedicates to refuting the Manichaean myth, but they are always considerable. The Catholic bishop knew how to skillfully use the caricature technique in his presentation of it. In it he usually found an additional argument, often a last argument, against the opponent's positions. In reality, he only applied to the myth the same procedures that Faust had applied against the Old Testament. An interpretation, extremely close to the literal tenor of the text, led in both cases to identical results, with identical satisfaction for the respective parties.

Augustine measures the texts of the Old Testament and those of Manes that contain the myth with a different standard, denying them the right to any type of symbolic interpretation. Augustine's diligence in denying it, basing himself on the fact that Manes, as the last revealer, had promised the pure and naked truth, seems to indicate that the Manicheans criticized him for the double measure used. On the other hand, the fact that Augustine has to resort to pagan praxis to justify its use in the Old Testament seems to indicate that the Manichaeans were not advocating it for their own myth, or in other words, that they were simply limiting themselves to censuring the behavior of the Catholics.

Augustine therefore makes a rigidly literal reading of the myth. But the deficiencies from the Manichean point of view do not end there. A text is deformed not only by changing the literal tenor of the words, but also by changing the key to reading; changing its semantics, frequently linked to the underlying logic or metaphysics.

Let's take specific cases. Augustine works with a Catholic metaphysics referring to God: that of absolute simplicity. In it all attributes are identified. From here, he will draw conclusions that the Manichaeans could not share. For example, according to the presbyter Fortunatus, the Manichaeans distinguished between Christ and the soul (C.Fortun. 12). According to Dr. Félix, the Manichaeans distinguish nature and substance in God, the second being a broader concept than the first (C.Felicem YU 15; C.Fortun. 11). Thus, the soul, which is a portion of God (pars Dei), is a portion of its substance, not of its nature. Well, Augustine, applying his Catholic metaphysics, ignores such distinctions, and nothing prevents him from first identifying the soul with God and then applying to God the mutations that the soul undergoes. The result obtained is that the God of the Manicheans is worse even than the patriarchs so denigrated by the Manicheans. The same can be stated regarding the identification established between Manés and the Holy Spirit, based on the fact that the former was considered the Paraclete. Whether it was conscious or unconscious, it is not easy to affirm **. The truth is that, as Felix and Fortunatus already did, the Manichaeans would not feel addressed by Augustine's accusations, even if the Catholics became more convinced of the absurdity of the Manichean doctrine.

The same Catholic metaphysics leads him to reproach the Manichaeans for their inability to show their God as unlimited (XV 5). A reproach that would fit a Catholic, never a Manichaean, since at the very core of his system

Other times, the intention is clearer. Well informed, it does not always inform well, in that it silences notable aspects. He has no qualms about presenting half-truths. But there is something else. As it could not be otherwise, given that it is a controversial work, Agustín forces the statements of his adversary. What he presents as a pure hypothesis, he takes as a pure statement, and then tries to urge him from it. Having rejected the Hebrew prophets, Faustus admits that, in the hypothesis that there were prophecies about Christ in the Gentiles, they could be of some use to them. As if he had stated it plainly and simply, Augustine calls on him to show him some (XIII 3). When he asks him to show him prophets who announced Christ, as they understand it, it is outside the positions of the Manichaean bishop (XIII 4). Likewise, he commits the fallacy of taking literally what the other puts as an image (eating the fish from the sea, but not the water) (XVI 19).

If Faust's exegesis is conditioned by dogma itself, Augustine's is no less so. In some circumstances, modern exegesis agrees with the Manichaean bishop and refutes that of Hippo. The case is given with reference to 2 Cor 4:4 (XXI 1-2). The same controversy leads him to sacrifice the novelty of the New Testament to the harmony between the two Testaments (XIX 28-29).

!* In the Augustinian anti-Manichean production, Manichaeans and Catholics dispute the title of Christian. From the Manichaeans who always present themselves as Christians, even more so, as authentic Christians, Augustine tries to strip them of this title, trying to show that their Christianity is fictitious. The event divided scholars in the past. Some, the undeniable Christian elements present in the documents that Augustine provides, considered them only as a covering with a view to the mission in Christianized territories. The discussion oscillated in one direction or another depending on the nature of the latest discoveries made. Currently, especially after the discoveries of the Kephalaia, Homilies and Psalms in the Coptic language and particularly in the light of the Mani Codex of Cologne, it cannot be denied that Christianity, although in a heterodox form, is at the very origins of Manichaeism. Augustine was only right to the extent that he measured Christianity from the postulates of the Catholic Church. Identifying Christianity and Catholicism, the Manichaeans were truly pseudo-Christians.

See, however, how easily the truth and sound doctrine answers, how easily it breaks this double and insurmountable bond of your question. Suppose someone, endowed with real power, threatens a Christian with hanging from a tree if he does not agree to worship the sun. “If I manage to escape, you say, from the curse cast by the law against whoever worships the sun, I will fall into the other, also cast by the law against whoever hangs on a tree.” That's where the confusion would come from, but for you or, better yet, not even for you who worship the sun, even without anyone forcing you. On the other hand, the Christian built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets considers each of the motives and each of the curses; He sees that one belongs to the mortal body, which is going to be suspended from a tree, and the other to the soul with which the sun is worshiped. For, although the body bows in the act of worship, it is the soul that worships what it worships or pretends to do so. Both are harmful. 1. Fausrus: —Why don't you accept the Old Testament?

—Because no full glass receives what is poured into it, but rather lets it fall, and the saturated stomach rejects more food. For this reason the Jews, monopolized by Moses and satisfied with the Old Testament, rejected the New, and we, warned by Christ and filled with the New, reject the Old. You, on the other hand, accept neither one nor the other, because you are not full of either, but only half full, with the particularity that in you one with the other is not filled but rather corrupted, since half glasses are never filled with contents of a different nature, but of the same or a similar nature, as wine with wine, honey with honey, and vinegar with vinegar. If you pour different contents and not of the same type, such as gall over honey, water over wine or oil over garo, this is not about filling, but about adulteration. Here is why we do not accept the Old Testament.

1. Faust: —Why do you not accept Moses, if Christ says: Moses wrote about me, and: If you believed Moses you would also believe in me?

—I wish that not only Moses, but all the Gentile and Jewish prophets had written about Christ. What harm would it bring to our faith, or rather, what benefit would it not bring to it, if we could gather coherent and adequate testimonies in favor of our God from everywhere? Because then, the hatred and execration of superstition remaining, we would be free to select from them only the prophecies referring to Christ. Indeed, I do not consider there to be a contradiction in the fact that even Moses, although a stranger to Christ, seems to have written something about him. Wouldn't every man wish to take flowers from every bramble, fruit from every plant, honey from every insect, even though we take neither insects nor grass as food, nor thorns as decoration for a crown? MEANING OF CIRCUMCISION

29. Furthermore, Christ would not testify so clearly in favor of that Sabbath which you mock for ignorance and impiety, if he were not included among the prophecies about Christ. As Faustus himself recognized, praising him, when Christ suffered of his own will, having, therefore, in his power to choose the time of his passion and resurrection, he made his flesh rest in the grave on Saturday, to manifest, by rising on the third day, the so-called Sunday, considered the eighth to follow the Sabbath, that circumcision on the eighth day also included a prophecy about itself. What does circumcision of the flesh mean? What else, but the dispossession of mortality that we carry as a consequence of carnal generation? Therefore the Apostle says: Putting off the flesh, he set an example for the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself. By saying that he put off the flesh, we understand that he refers to the mortality of the flesh, according to which this body is properly called flesh. That mortality is properly called flesh, because it will not exist in that immortality of the resurrection. That is why it is written: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. Regarding these futurum numquam habuit requiem, quia numquam securus Fuit, qui se cogitabat tam graue bellum cum tanta membrorum suorum labe damnoque gesturum?

20.8 L.20. Who are pagans 437 local separation does not occur except in the bodies? If you knew this, you would never have spun so many fables with your foolish and senseless imagination. Therefore, if the heat were in the sun, at the same time that the moon stood out for its light, in any case these fantastic creations would have found the fog of verisimilitude to deceive animal and carnal men, who think that nothing exists other than what, in their opinion, is corporeal. In fact, the force of heat acts to move, so they would attribute it to Power; On the other hand, since the clear radiance of light operates the manifestation, they would attribute it to Wisdom. But since it is the sun that stands out greatly for its light, how do they place Power in it, while placing Wisdom in the moon, which shines much less? Oh sacrilegious ignorance! Since the only Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, and the Holy Spirit is distinct from Christ, how is Christ himself separated from himself, if the Holy Spirit is not separated from him? You show that the air, to which your fable assigns as the seat of the Holy Spirit, fills the entire fabric of the world. Therefore, the sun and the moon are always with him when they travel their orbits. On the other hand, the moon moves away and approaches, in alternating periods, with respect to the sun. Thus, considering you as authors or, better, as deceivers, Wisdom moves away from Power during half of its journey and returns to it again in the other half. And when it is full, Wisdom is far from Power; So these two stars are separated possint? Quod si sciretis, numquam stulto insanoque phantasmate so many fables texeretis. In ea!

It is true that pagans also have certain fictions of a fabulous nature, but they recognize them as fables, because they either affirm that they were created by poets to delight, or they try to interpret them as referring to the nature of things or the customs of men?! Thus they speak of Vulcan's lameness, due to its similarity to the movement of earthly fire; of the blindness of Fortune, because things that are called fortuitous happen in an unforeseeable way; of the three Fairies who with the distaff, the spindle and the fingers twist the woolen thread, with reference to the three times: the past, what is already spun, what has passed from the distaff to use; the present, which passes through the fingers of the spinner, and the future existing in the wool placed on the spinning wheel, which still has to pass through the fingers of the spinner until use, as through the present towards the future. Do they also talk about Venus, as a woman quid de ceteris uestris fabulis dicam? Quis enim splenditenens suspendit mundum et quis Atlas cum illo subportat? 20.10 L.20. Who are pagans 443 fit in one section, applying another criterion, it will move to another where it was not before. Let's take an example: if someone classifies all flesh beings into volatile and non-volatile, by virtue of this differentiating criterion, quadrupeds are more similar to men than to birds, since they are united by not being able to fly. If, in turn, the criterion of rationality is applied, some beings are rational, others irrational; In this case, quadrupeds are more similar to birds than to men: they are united by being deprived of reason.

Not considering this fact, Faustus says: "But if you look for sects there are only two: that of the Gentiles and ours, since we think very differently from how they think." That is: because he had said that the Gentiles differed from the Manichaeans above all in the affirmation that everything proceeds from a beginning, something which the Manichaeans deny, adding the beginning of the race of darkness. In this differentiating criterion—it must be recognized—most pagans think the same as us. But Faustus did not see that, in turn, if someone established another classification, stating that of those who follow another religion, some like to worship a single God and others to worship many, by virtue of this new differentiating criterion, the pagans are very far from us, the Manichaeans included in the same group as the pagans, and we in that of the Jews. 502 Against Faustus 22,2 I now call a law not to circumcision, nor to the Sabbaths, sacrifices and other things of the kind, but to that which is truly a law, that is: You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not swear falsely, etc. This law was already spread among the Gentiles from ancient times, that is, since the creation of this world existed. Breaking into it, the Hebrew writers interpolated these precepts, abhorrent as leprosy and scabies and dishonest to the maximum, referring to circumcision and sacrifices.

Cheer up! If you are also truly a friend of the law, condemn with me those who dared to violate said law by adding to it those precepts that do not conform to it. If you did not also know that these precepts are not the law, nor a part of the law, you would either strive to fulfill them, having professed to live according to justice, or you would publicly confess that you are not righteous. Now, however, you, with reference to those who want to live according to justice, worry carefully about those precepts that prohibit criminal behavior, but you do not mention in the least those that refer to the Jews. To what extent are you excusable for this procedure, unless it is clear that they are not part of the law? Finally, in the event that someone calls you uncircumcised or objects to you for neglecting the Sabbath precept, if you become enraged just as you are irritated and consider it an intolerable insult for someone to tell you that you ignore the precept of no circumcisionem nec sabbata et sacrificia ceteraque huiusmodi ludaeorum, sed eam, quae uere sit lex, id est: Non occides, non moechaberis, non peiurabis (Ex 15,13ff) et cetera. 22.3 L.22. Morality of the Patriarchs and Prophets 503 to kill or not to commit adultery, it could be understood that you consider both things to be the law and command of God. But now, with respect to the first, you seek the praise and glory of preserving it, and with respect to the second, you do not in the least fear the loss of that good, since you despise it.

Therefore, as I said, it is clear that these precepts are not part of the law, but rather are stains and scabs of it. If we condemn them, we condemn them for being false, not for belonging to the law. And this insult does not affect the law or God its author, but rather those who put the name of God and the law in their impious religions. If we sometimes attack the venerable term "law" when we pursue the precepts of the Jews, it is your fault that you do not want to make any distinction between the Hebrew institutions and the law. Otherwise, restore the law's own dignity, remove, as if they were warts, Israelite clumsiness, impute to the writers the serious fault of having distorted it, and you will instantly see that we have been enemies of Judaism, not of the law. It is the term that has deceived you, because you do not know to whom it should be rightly assigned.

DEFINITION OF SIN

27. Sin is a fact, saying or desire against the eternal law." In turn, the eternal law is the reason or divine will that commands the preservation of the natural order and prohibits altering it *. It is necessary to investigate, therefore, what the natural order is in man.

Man consists of soul and body, as does the animal. No one doubts that, due to the order of their natures, the soul must be put before the body. But reason is present in the soul of man, which the animal lacks. Therefore, as the soul is put before the body, so the reason of the soul itself is put before its remaining parts by the law of nature, esse, quae non sunt, nec tamen in eis eminent aliqua exempla virtutum, haec quoque intueamur, [621] quam ob causam illis inserta sint litteris, quas ad utilitatem uitae praesentis regendae et Futurae adipiscendae conditas salubriter credimus. Porro autem quaecumque in factis sanctorum elucent documenta ¡ustitiae nullus uel inperitorum dubitat debuisse conscribi. De illis ergo potest esse quaestio, quae uel inaniter scripta uideri possunt, si nec recte facta adparent nec peccata sunt, uel etiam perniciose, si peccata esse conuincuntur, ne ualeant ad imitationem, siue in ipsis libris reprehensa non sint et ideo putari etiam possint non esse peccata, siue illic quoque reprehensa sint, sed sub facili spe ueniae committantur, quía et in sanctis inuenta sunt.

52. I consider that the two free women of Jacob are understood to refer to the New Testament in which we have been called to freedom; but it is not in vain that there are two. 82. I have already reviewed all the people that Faust used to accuse the Old Testament Scripture. To each case I have dedicated the appropriate speech, with which I have either defended the men of God against the accusations of heretics and carnal men, or, having reproached men, I have shown that Scripture is praiseworthy and venerable.

Let us now see, in the order in which Faustus mentioned these men when accusing them, what they prophesy or what they announce as the future. I already did it with respect to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who wanted to be called God, as if it were only their God who is God of all creation. He had not granted them such a great honor in vain, if he had not seen in them the authentic and full love that only he could know in a perfect and supreme way, and if in a certain way he had not consummated in said three fathers the great and admirable mystery of his future people. In fact, using free women - this is the case of Sarah, Rebekah, Leah and Rachel - they fathered not only for freedom, but also for slavery - from the same Rebekah Esau was born, to whom it was said: You will be your brother's slave -, and, in turn, using slave women - which is the case of Hagar - they fathered not only for slavery, but also for freedom - the case of Bala and Zelpha. 93. Investigating the meaning of the previous action of burning the calf, crushing it, scattering it in the water and giving it to the people to drink requires greater attention. He was able to break the tables that he received, written with the finger of God, that is, with the action of the Holy Spirit, because he judged that they were not worth reading. He was able to hand the calf over to the fire, crush it, scatter it and immerse it in the water, so that it would completely disappear from his presence. But for what purpose did he give it to the people to drink? Who does not feel stimulated to investigate and understand its prophetic meaning? Let the calf be presented to attentive minds as the body of the devil, that is, the men of all peoples who, with reference to these sacrileges, have the devil as their head, that is, as their inspiration. And precisely golden calf because the idolatrous rites seem as if instituted by wise men. The Apostle says of them: Because recognizing him as God, they did not glorify him as they gave thanks to God, but rather they became confused in their reasoning and their foolish hearts were darkened; Saying that they were wise, they became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for a representation in the form of corruptible man, of birds, of quadrupeds, of reptiles. GENITAL MEMBERS ARE NOT CLUMPY

4. Far be it from us to think that there is any clumsiness in the members of the saints, even if they are the genitals! Indeed, they are called dishonest because they do not have the same beautiful appearance as the other members that are visible *. But see what the Apostle says, when he persuades the Church of the unity and connection of the members of our body. It says: The members that seem to be the weakest in the body are indispensable. And those who seem to be the most vile in the body, we surround with greater honor. Thus we dress our dishonest parts with greater honesty, because our honest parts do not need it. God has formed the body by giving more honor to the members that lacked it, so that there would be no division in the body.

The illicit use and not subject to the laws of temperance of said members is clumsy, not the members themselves, which celibates and virgins preserve in wonderful integrity. The holy married fathers and mothers themselves used them, thinking only of procreation, so that the natural movement that does not serve lasciviousness, but rather reason, is not at all clumsy. Therefore how much less clumsy were these members in the Virgin Mary who conceived the flesh of Christ by faith! They did not even serve human and licit conception, but exclusively the birth of God. No wonder sicut mortem simulatam, sed prorsus nullam praedicare uoluisse in consequenti sermone adparebit, ubi alteri responderbimus quaestioni.

The First Man occupies an important place in the Manichean myth. But it must be placed in the whole, since it is just one more in the series of figures that follow one another as evocations or emanations, since Augustine does not mention them all. Its designation varies according to the different languages ​​in which the documents have reached us and which can be seen in M. Tardieu (Le Manicháisme, p.104-105) or also in A. Bóhlig (Die Ghosts. 11] Der Manicháismus, p.61-61). This First Man is the son of God the Father and the Mother of life (ignored in Augustinian work and equal to the Spirit in some texts) with whom he forms a Trinity (cf. Á. BÓHLIG, Die Gnosis UI, p.30). In fact, God, the Lord of the kingdom of light, foreseeing that it was going to be attacked by his antagonist, the Prince of the Kingdom of darkness, evokes from his own substance the Mother of life and this, in turn, the First Man. This has nothing to do with Adam, who was made of flesh and blood, since he is of divine substance. It is the first in the series of three envoys or messengers of God. God sends him to defend his kingdom from the planned attack of the princes of evil, who upon seeing the light of the neighboring kingdom felt the desire to invade it (X 3; XXI 10). The Manichean presbyter Fortunatus resorts to an evangelical image: he was sent like a lamb in the midst of wolves (Mt 10:16). To confront them, he evokes his five children, the five elements. Equipped with them he approached the enemy kingdom. When the prince of demons and his army saw him, they rushed against him, defeated him, and devoured him. The First Man had sacrificed himself for the good of the entire kingdom of light, paying a very high price. The light that was him mixed with the darkness and likewise his elements were mixed and contaminated by contact with matter. He lost all his consciousness, remaining as if asleep, ignorant of his true being.

But what seemed like a victory for the princes of evil became the beginning of their defeat, as they had admitted within themselves the adverse principle that would act as a corrosive principle or poison (XX 17; XXI 13). The First Man had been like a bait set by God to capture them (XX 17). For this reason, what seemed like a defeat by God was nothing more than a first stage in a long-term process to contain his antagonist within his limits.

The loss of consciousness had not been absolute. A part of that divine substance regained consciousness and invoked the Father. God felt compassion and determined to free the First Man. To do this, he proceeds to a new series of emanations: God evokes the Friend of the lights; this to the great Architect, and this, lastly, to the powerful Spirit (in Augustine's terminology; living, in other sources: Cf. Keph. 16,49,24; 17,56,8, 19,60,21; Psalm 233,11,13; T. bar Khonai [A. Apam, Texte, p.17; A. BÓHLIG, Die Gnosis HI, p.104]). The Friend of the lights and the living Spirit descended into the land of darkness. From there the powerful Spirit called to the First

Man. The latter's response followed his call, waking up from his lethargy. Then the same powerful Spirit stretched out his hand and freed him from the clutches of matter. Thus he returned to the Mother of life and then to the Father. Liberation had taken place, although not complete. In effect, the First Man emerged stripped of his "garment", his five elements, which remained captive to Evil. If the world exists it is because God designed it to seek the liberation of those elements (cf. complementary note 6). It was an element of Manichaean faith that appeared in the directories of confession (cf. W. BANG, Manichaische, p.145). In any case, the figure of the First Man is not Manés' invention. It had clear parallels in other Gnostic systems (cf. K. RunoLr, Maní und díe Gnosís: P. BRYDERS (ed.) Manichaean Studies, p.197).

Returning to the data that Agustín provides us, it is appropriate to highlight some aspects. First of all, it is evident that it does not offer all the chain soaps, nor does it narrate all the adventures of the First Man. Of the first series of evocations, he silences the Mother of Life, as well as the Great Architect of the second. Augustine oversimplifies by attributing to him the formation of the world, which is not properly his work. He is also silent about the form of his liberation and the initial liberation itself. It only refers to the liberation process that takes place in history. As befits a polemicist, he accentuates negative aspects: its coating of deceptive elements, the lamentable state in which these were left.

To our knowledge, Augustine is the only one who provides the explicit information that they considered Jesus Christ to be the son of the First Man. There is nothing strange about it from the title that he gave himself of "Son of Man", which is, for the Manichaeans, that First Man, and from Manichaean Christology.

Augustine's criticism takes two directions. On the one hand, highlighting that everything is the work of his imagination and fantasy. The term he usually uses is commentitium. On the other hand, showing that there is no First Man other than the one mentioned by Paul and that he has nothing to do with the Manichean First Man.

Being so central to the Manichean system, the data appears, in one form or another, in all sources. But these "elements" do not always receive the same name. Augustine further designates them as "limbs", "clothes" or "armor" (XI 3). M. Tardieu (Le Manicheisme, p.105-105) tells us the other names it receives in the different regions and languages, namely: the five gods, the five lights, the children of light, the five bodies, the splendours, the immortal saints, the soul or the I, the good soul; the living soul, the luminous I, the living I, God of what really exists. Various names, then, but constancy in the quinary number (the last examples cited do not claim a numerical designation). Such elements, to continue with Augustinian terminology, are the following: water, fire, wind, air and light (II 3). The variations from one source to another are minimal: some use the breeze instead of the air. Each of them has a pneumatic and a psychic aspect. Thus air is related to intelligence and love; the wind with science and faith; the light with thought and perfection; water with reflection and patience, and fire with consciousness and wisdom (C£. R. MERKELBACH, Das Manicháische System. Vortrage / Rheinisch-Westfálische Akademie der Wissenschaften, G. 281 [Opladen 1986], p.20).

A Manichean directory for confession says of such elements: "The five gods are the Majesty and the radiance, the appearance and the figure, the body and the soul, the force and the light, the foundation at the root of everything that exists on earth" (W. BANG, Manichaische, p.149). Augustine emphasizes that they are of the substance of God (X1,3). On the one hand they are a participation in the "virtues" present in God (cf. complementary note 4); on the other, they identify with every living soul. From another point of view, they are the positive counterpart of the same elements present in the kingdom of darkness in a negative version. If in two cases the contrast takes place through different substances (light/darkness; air/smoke), in the remaining three it only takes place through the qualification of the same substance (pure wind, water and fire/impure wind, water and fire) (II 3; De haeres. 46,7). In combat each element opposed its respective opponent. Augustine objects to them that, in practice, the presentation of the myth is reduced to the struggle of light against darkness (H 3).

One particular deserves to be highlighted, Augustine highlights that the First Man resorts to cunning to achieve his objectives (11 4; V 4.5; VI 8). Knowing their gluttony of the prince of the opposite kingdom, he transforms the elements with which he had clothed himself (cf. In An Nabim, 41 Fibrist: A. BOHLIG, Die Gnosis 1H, p.146) into a kind of bait, and thus deceives them. In the words of Titus de Bostra: "The good Being sends a power that apparently was supposed to guard its borders, but which in reality was a bait destined to capture the devil" (Against Manichaeos. Cited by P. ALFARIC, L'évolution intellectuel de saint Augustin. 1. Du platonisme au christianisme, Paris 1918, p.104, n. 2). This is the reason why Augustine alludes to them as deceptive elements (11 4; V 4; VL8; X1,3).

These elements suffered the same fate as the First Man they covered. In fact, although it ultimately resolves in victory, never complete - Augustine will insist again and again (16; III 6; VI 6; XXI 14.15; XIX 24) -, they are defeated, they are devoured, they mix with matter and, as a consequence, they remain defiled, on the one hand (11 5; V 7; VI 3.4.8; VII 2; XI 3; XIII 18; XX 17.19.22; XXI 22.98; XXXII 19.22; C. Fel. 11.3.7.11.13.15.16.19.

As the world was formed for its liberation, its particles, which like them are of the substance of God, are scattered throughout everything that exists (cf. supplementary note 7). It is necessary that they recover knowledge about themselves, which will happen thanks to gnosis. All of this will guide the same Manichean morality in its contents.

[6] The formation of the world (15).—Neither Faust nor Felix provide us with any information about this section of the myth, undoubtedly because they knew that it was an easy object of criticism, if not ridicule, of their opponents. But we can reconstruct it with what Agustín gives us, corroborated and completed by those obtained from other sources.

In the Manichean myth the formation, not creation, of the world is not an absolutely free act of God. It is his decision that, we can say, arises from a kind of moral obligation to free a part of his substance, which in order to defend his Kingdom of Light, were devoured by the inhabitants of the Kingdom of darkness (cf. complementary note 4). That is, to the elements of the First Man (cf. complementary note 3) that, once he was freed, remained prisoners of matter.

The world or cosmos is a gigantic structure designed by God to achieve this liberation. Although made by God, its materials come from the kingdom of darkness. God ordered the First Man, the great Architect and the living (or powerful in Augustine's terminology: XX 9) Spirit with his five sons (cf. supplementary note 24) to confront the race of darkness in war, subdue it, and build the world with it. Once the battle was engaged, victory fell to the forces of the Kingdom of light. These killed the leaders (archons) of the opposite kingdom and with them organized the world (H 5; VÍ 8; XX 9; Psalm 223,10,23-24; Seven Chapters 3,77-78 [S.N.C. Liu, An Early Byzantine Formula, p.180.203). With their bodies they formed eight lands (XXXII 19; T. bar Khonai LA. Abam, Texte, p.19; A. BóHLIG, Die Gnosis HI, p.1051; Psalm 223,10,26; Keph. 47,118,24) and with their bones the rocks (XV 4). Once skinned, with their skins the Mother of life (cf. supplementary note 3) made ten firmaments (XXXII 19; Psalm 223,10,25; Keph. 44,115,7; 47,118,20; 54,131,24) or eleven (thus T. bar Khonai, ¿b). Meats and wine are, in turn, the dregs and gall of the race of darkness (XVI 31; De »moribus 1 16,44; De haeres. 46,11). Some of the archons of darkness were nailed to the heavenly vault, which is why, when they are not illuminated by the sun or the moon, they appear dark, except

the little points of light (the stars) that are the particles of light that they had devoured. The bad waters were gathered in one place, thus giving rise to the ocean that surrounds the earth; likewise the bad fire and the smoke were enclosed in large tanks around the ocean. As the kingdom of darkness had devoured the elements of the First Man, particles of light are present throughout the universe, although at different levels.
Most of the light was found in the semen of the archons. Once released by means that never fail to attract attention (cf. XV 7; XX

6.8; C. Fel, Y 7; De natura boni 44; Of haeres. 46,8.11; complementary note 26), was concentrated and distilled. Of the purest, the powerful Spirit created the sun and the moon (cf. supplementary note 15); with the one that follows in purity, the stars. With luminous substance likewise, the great Architect built three wheels: that of fire around which the sun rotates, that of water around which the moon rotates and that of the wind that is identified with the Zodiac (cf.

774 Supplementary notes 17). The axles of the three wheels are formed by particles of light so fine that they cannot be perceived. The axis on which the Zodiac rotates is called the "Pillar of Praise" or "Perfect Man" (Eph 4:13). Also

The other two wheels have luminous axles. The three axes, together with their radii, form giant crosses that are in the firmament: "The cross of light." All those particles of light are parts of the First Man.
Once the universe was formed, the living Spirit entrusted its preservation to his five sons (cf. supplementary note 24). Cf. R. MERKELBACH, Mani, p.22-24.

[7] The "lesus patibilis" (XX 2.11),—Augustine twice refers to three different aspects of Manichean Christology. In the first he questions Faust: «Tell us how many Christs you affirm exist. Is it one that generates the earth by conceiving of the Holy Spirit..., another that whom the Jews crucified in the time of Pontius Pilate, and a third that extends through the sun and the moon? (XX 11). And a little later: "If you affirm that Jesus is in the trees, that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate and that he extends through the sun and the moon, because all of this comes from a single substance..." (ibid.). Such is the triple aspect: a) Jesus patibilis; b) the historical Jesus; c) the cosmic Jesus. In this note we deal with the first of them; leaving for notes 31 and 32 respectively the consideration of the other two.

The expression lesus patíbilis only appears in the pen of Faust (XX 2) and then in Augustine's reply (XX 11). This has led several authors, in past times, to maintain that such teaching constitutes a peculiarity of Numidian Manichaeism, at the service of missionary activity. L. H. Grondijs wrote: «En Afrique proconsulaire, Pexpression lesus patibilis trahissait Pintention de prolonger la confussion et le camouflage de la doctrine secréte. Mais la confiscation des livres destinés aux Élus ne permettait plus de prolonger le malentendu, et il fut dorénavant facile aux évéques chrétiens de démasquer leurs adversaires» (Analyse du manicháisme numidien au IV* siécle: Augustinus Magister 1954, t. 3, p.408-410, specifically 409; cf. the refutation made by E. DECRET, Aspects, p.284, n.2). The Dutch author has not been the only one to defend this thesis. He had been preceded by K. Kessler (Mani. Manichier: Realencyklopádie fiir protestantische Theologie und Kirche, Ed. by A. Hauck [Leipzig 19031, XII 208), H.J. Polotsky (Manicháismus: Paulus Realencyklopádie der klassischen Alterthumwissenschaften, Ed. by W. Kroll. Supplement VI [Stuttgart 19351, 259) and C. Colpe (Die religiongeschichliche Schule. Darstellung und Kritik ibres Bildes von gnostischen Erlosermitbos: R. BULTMANN (ed.), Forschungen zur E nd Literatur des Alten Testamentes, NE 60 (Góttingen 1961), p.178179].

This thesis was already rejected by F. Cumont (Recherches sur le Mamicháisme. 1 La Cosmogonie manichéenne d'apres Théodore bar Khonai, [Bruxelles 1908], p.48) who has been followed by others later. In fact, a series of testimonies prove that the conception of Jesus patibilis must have been part of the doctrine of Manés himself, although the expression regarding it was probably linked to North Arica. The same idea of lesus patibilis is found in Bar Khonai's Liber Scholiorum (A. Abam, Texte, p.22; A. BÓHLIG, Die Gnosis III, p.108); Alexander of Licópolis also speaks of the dynamis patbetiké (Contre la doctrine de Mani, 8: 32 [Paris 1985] p.79) which must be understood in that sense. We have the clearest document on this matter in the CMC (10,4-5; 96,21-- 97,10; cf. A. Henricus-L. KoENEN, Ein griechiscber Mani-Codex: ZEP 5 [1970] p.147, n.130-131 and p.150-151), which "has shown that the doctrine of lesus patibilis does not mean any own particular development of

Additional notes 775 completed regions» (A. BÓHLIG, Zur religionsgeschichtlichen Einordnung des Manicbáismus: P. BRYDER [ed.], Manichaean Studies, p.44). The Coptic texts, for their part, testify to the same doctrine, although with different terminology. To refer to the suffering light they speak of the "cross of light" (Keph. 85,208213). Although they do not explicitly link the cross of light to the cross of Jesus, this connection must have been an original Manichean doctrine from the time the Gnostic parallels do so (N.A. PEDERSEN, Early, p-185). To all this we must add other texts of Eastern Manichaeism (cf. A. BÓBLIG, Die Gnosis YI, p.58) and certain aspects of the behavior of the Manichaeans that derive from said doctrine, specifically hand seal (cf. F. DÉcrEr, Aspects, p. 12-13).

This lesus patibilis can be represented, with the words of N.A. Pedersen, in the following way: «The imprisoned Light is found in the earth, but under the influence of the Holy Spirit, that is, the power of light and heat, it rises to the plants, accumulates in the roots, passes higher through delicate channels and finally concentrates in the flowers and fruits. From the color, brightness and smell of Hores and fruits it is possible to deduce the amount of light they contain" (Early, p.175). Augustine, for his part, writes: "They believe that herbs and trees live in such a way that they believe that the life that is in them is sensitive, and that they feel pain when they are damaged: so that no one can tear or break off anything from them without causing them suffering" (De haeres. 46,12; cf. also the Adiman. 22). Hence the prohibition of giving bread to a non-Manichean beggar (VI 5; 10,18) they cry. But its suffering presence is not limited to plants, but also extends to animals, stars in the sky, and even to man, that is, to the human soul (15; V 6; VI 4.5.6; XV 4; XVI 9; XX 17.20; XXII 71; XXI 10). Hence the "worship" that they professed to the entire universe (XX 2).

This lesus patibilis is not identified, therefore, with the historical Jesus (cf. complementary note 31), but with the pars dei, with that divine portion, which is imprisoned in matter. Since the latter belongs to the opposite race, it becomes its particular cross. Hence they speak of him hanging on every tree (XX 2), or that he is crucified in the whole world and in the whole soul (XXXU 7; Secund. [3]; Enarr. in ps. 140,12; ALEXANDER OF LICOPOLIS, Contra la doctrine de Mani, 32), or the affirmation that Christ is born, suffers and dies daily (Evobro, De fide 34). If they allow themselves to speak of "crucifixion" they do so based on the double meaning of the Greek term hyle: matter and forest/wood (De natura boní 18). Likewise, this last meaning must be related to the fact that the princes of demons bring their origin from the five trees, which come from the five elements (VI 8) and from which animals are in turn born (XXI 12). Consequently, to affirm that light is mixed with matter is equivalent to saying that it is Sucified on a tree. This mixture is the cross of light (Exarr. in ps. 140,12; c£. Keph. 85,208-213). The lesus patíbilis truly suffers both the flagellation and the other sufferings of the scaffold. The tragedy of Golgotha ​​takes place in the entire nature. It is not difficult to understand that if they talk about the passion of Jesus it is only as an accommodation to a Christian environment.
The liberation of this passion takes place thanks to the work of the "elect" (cf. supplementary note 8).

According to W. Geerlings, Augustine preferred to center his Christology on the incarnation and not on the Cross and the resurrection, to distance himself from the Manichean lesus patibilis (Der manicháische "Jesus patibilis" in der Theologie Augustins: Theological Quartalschrift 152 [1972] 124-131), a thesis that does not

[8] The "elect" (IL 5).—All members of the Manichean Church belonged to one of these two categories, or professiones (De haeres. 46,5), gradus (Thebesa Manuscript [=MT] II 2,2.10; UI 2,6, etc.; De moribus 1 18,65), or ordines (MT 12,8): to that of the "hearers" or to the of the "elect"

They constitute the one Church, as inseparable parts (F. DECRET, Aspects de l'Eglise Manichéenne. Remarques sur le Manuscrit de Tébessa: Signum Pietatis. Festgabe fiir Cornelius Petrus Mayer, Augustinus-Verlag, [Würzburg 1989], 123-151, p.136). The difference in degrees does not respond to two different types of Gnostic initiation, but to two different levels of it (F. Décrer, Mani, p.113). The "elect" were also designated by the name of perfect (MT VI 1,6.15), saints (Comf. IV 1,1), just (MT III 2,16), or "virgins" (Pilgrims' Psalm 179,13ff). Denominations taken from the New Testament (for the elect, cf. Col 3:12; Eph 1:3-4; 1 Cor 26-27, Mt 22:14; for the perfect: Phil 3:15; 1 Cor 2:6; Eph 6:13; Col 4:12; Mt 5:48; for saints, passim).

However, that of the "elect" represented a higher level. In fact, all members of The Hierarchy belonged to him. In his only reference to her, Faust speaks of the genus sacerdotale (XXX 4). Hierarchy that was constituted, in clausí numbers, by a single supreme leader (princeps) (legitimate successor of Manés, after Sisinnio, Innaio, etc.), 12 teachers, 72 bishops with their deacons, and 360 priests (De haeres. 46,16; Epist. 236,2). To them must be added those who perform other minor functions or "ministries", such as choir teachers, preachers, scribes and singers (cf. M. TarDizU, Le manicháisme, p.77-79, who includes the different designations they receive in different places). But the number of "hierarchs" was not identified with that of the "elect." This was not clausus, and was always open to desirable new additions of men and women. In fact, the number was small, even compared only to the faithful of the sect, a fact understandable from the high moral demands, since they had chosen to walk the narrow path spoken of in the gospel, fulfilling the advice of Jesus (Mt 7,13-14; 19,21.29; 10,9-10; Luke 12,22; cf. MT). They justified this numerical requirement by resorting to Mt 22,14 ("many are called and few are chosen") (cf. MT III 1,15-17). In the same New Testament they found their rototypes, particularly Saint Paul, especially regarding his missionary activity, and Mary of Bethany, who had chosen the best part (Lk 10,42. Cf. MT 112,1 and CMC 92,14-93,2. Also F. Décrer, Aspects de l'Eglise, p.135-142).

We do not know that there was a special rite of entry into said order. In any case it exceeded a personal decision, and the approval of the sect authorities was required. Perhaps an anointing confirmed the "elect" who would leave for missionary work in their mission (Psalm 227,22,11-12).
The status of clergy was linked to a strict rule of sanctity. The best known are the three seals that had to be kept scrupulously.

[10] Metempsychosis (II 5).—None of the three members of the Manichean hierarchy whose controversy with Augustine has reached us, that is, Fortunatus, Faustus and Felix, make any reference to this point of the Manichean faith, which the Bishop of Hippo attributes directly to Manes (auctorem ipsum vestrum: De moribus 1 17,55). He speaks of it, in fact, in his Book of Secrets, according to Al-Biruni, who points out that it is a loan he took from India (cf. M.H. BrowDER, A/-Biruni's Manichaean Sources: P. BRYDER [ed.], Manichaean Studies, p.21). Yes, however, the listener Secundino. In his letter to Augustine he uses it to instill fear in him: "Cease, he tells him, from enclosing Christ in a womb (=believing that he was born of a woman), so as not to see yourself enclosed again in another womb" (Epist. Secund. [51). With such words the Roman listener confirms these others from Augustine: "It is known that you, that is, your founder, usually threaten, as if it were a great punishment, although not the maximum, with reincarnation in a tree" (De moribus Y 17,55). The maximum punishment referred to may refer either to a possibility within metempsychosis (for example, being reborn in an animal instead of in a tree) or to another outside of it (exclusion of the very possibility of reincarnation).

It is true that metempsychosis is an enormous punishment (ingens poena: De moribus 1 17,55) compared to the other alternative, reserved for the "elect." Once their earthly journey in fidelity has concluded, their good souls pass on to the celestial ships that take them to their place of origin, the Kingdom of light (XX 21). But, even admitting this punitive nature, metempsychosis has the positive character of being a new opportunity given to "listeners" to achieve full purification. Their very belonging to that degree indicates that they did not accept to completely separate themselves from the ties of matter. On two occasions Augustine explicitly links metempsychosis with the "listeners" (V 10; De haeres. 46,12). Possibility that they are excluded, and this is the supreme punishment (summa poena: De moribus Y 17,55; graviores poenae: Faust XX 21) who, going down the path of infidelity, renounce following the path of gnosis. In the Manichean conception, metempsychosis (or transmigration [metaggismós] is not simply identified with reincarnation, in the proper sense of the term. The term used by Augustine is revolutio. Reincarnation as such is only a possibility and not the most desirable. Augustine mentions various types of revobrios. according to their term: "elect" (De haeres. 46,12); animals (pecora) (C. Adiman. 12,1); trees (De moribus II 17,55), melons, cucumbers and other vegetables (V 10). That is, the ways in which they can return to contact with matter are multiple (in aliis atque alios rerum corporalium formis: 11 5);

[12] The bodily resurrection (IV 2).—As happens on so many other points, the Manichaeans, always anchored in traditional Christian terminology, proclaim the resurrection. But the difference is substantial with respect to how the Catholic Church understands it. In fact, they only admit the resurrection of souls, while they reject, in the most absolute way, that of bodies (IV 2; XI 3). Nothing more in tune with the remaining doctrinal principles of the sect.

Saint Paul relates our resurrection to that of Christ (1 Cor 15:12-17). Consequently, rejecting the resurrection of Christ implies leaving that of other men without an apostolic argumentative basis. This is what the Manichaeans do when they affirm that, since he lacked a body in which to die, he could not be resurrected (XI 3; c£. supplementary note 31).

On the other hand, the traditional doctrine of the resurrection entails a qualitatively significant improvement of the body. According to St. Paul, it is sown in weakness, it is raised in strength; a psychic body is sown" and a spiritual body is resurrected (1 Cor 15:44). A fact that is impossible for the Manichaeans to accept, given that the body, because it belongs to the kingdom of darkness and is matter, and therefore radical evil, is metaphysically incapable of receiving any positivity.

Finally, they repeat, Paul said very clearly that neither flesh nor blood will inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor 15:50) (XI 3; C. Fortun. 19). Such words close every door of access for the body to the kingdom of God.

For its part, the resurrection of souls occurs through the preaching of the truth and, in turn, it is not an eschatological reality, but an actual one (unc) (IV 2). The soul is resurrected when it awakens from the sleep of death in which it finds itself as a consequence of immersion in matter. The announcement of the Manichean gnosis, carried out by the "elect" of the sect, is the condition of possibility of said resurrection.

sensitive and intelligible (De duabus an. 19), is what the Manichaeans constitute in diverse souls: the upper soul, a divine portion, directly related to the mind, and the lower soul, which is situated at the level of flesh and matter, and which perfectly explains the inner conflict in man. While the good soul has pneuma, the bad soul is nothing more than an irrational psyche.

A particular problem is raised by the terminology used by Augustine in both Conf. and De haeres 46. The first text speaks of the Manichaeans who "by noticing two wills in deliberation, affirm that there are two natures, to which the two minds correspond, one good and one bad." That is, the two ima have become two "minds." In the second text, Augustine presents the two designations as alternatives: two souls or two minds, one good and one bad, in conflict in the same man. The difficulty comes from the designation of the bad soul as "mind." Can a "mind" be attributed to the prince of darkness? Does he enjoy the light of the spirit and his intelligence? To speak like this is equivalent to attributing to him a rational soul, not just a vital principle that "animates" the movements of the body and the appetites of instinct.

The problem is solely one of terminology, but not in the sense that Augustine expressed himself imprecisely, which does not seem to be the case. It is only necessary to remove the specific meaning that it usually has in Augustinian philosophy from the term "mind" and give it a more generic guiding principle. Indeed, other Manichean sources testify in favor of the terminology used by Augustine. According to the Letter of the Foundation, the prince of darkness has around him innumerable other princes of which he is the "mind" and the origin (C. foundation epist. 15,19). Now, if in the macrocosm the race of darkness is guided and "inspired" by the evil "mind" of its prince, in man, the microcosm, the evil substance works through the flesh, which is guided by a "mind" that instils into it the appetite for concupiscence. Bad "mind" that presides over the internal conflict to subdue the good "mind." «There are therefore in every man two souls, or rather two contrary “minds” that have nothing in common except their name.
