[18] Manes, the Paraclete (VII 2).—Only once does Faustus mention Manes by name: in 12, where he designates him as “our father Manes”; In the other cases he limits himself to indicating him as "my teacher" (XIX 5: praeceptori meo), "our theologian" (XX 3) and the "Paraclete" (XXXII 6). More abundant in information is Augustine in his reply. Here we limit ourselves to one of the two most significant pieces of information that he gives us about him, namely, that he posed as the Paraclete, promised by Jesus (On the other, which refers to his sutodesignation as an apostle of Jesus Christ, cf. complementary note 22).

Multiple attestations of this data appear in Augustinian work, both in Contra Faustum (in addition to VI 2, cf. XIII 17; indirectly C. Fortun 22). Among the extra-Augustinian sources it is worth noting the Gospel of Manés itself, according to the testimony of Al-Biruni (A. Abam, Texte, 1); CMC 17.2-7; 46.1-3; 63,16-23; 70,17-23; Acta Archelai (13.28 PG 10,1451.1472); Evopio

Supplementary notes 789 (De fide 24); Seven Chapters (S.N.C. Lieu, An Early Byzantine Formula, p. 176.191); Keph. 1,14,4-11.32; 15,19-20; 16,29-30; Psalm 227, 20,19-24; 236,34,19; 35.14; 238,38,13 etc. The fact that the data is particularly abundant in Western sources has led some scholars to maintain that the identification of Manes with the Paraclete was an innovation, due to missionary demands, of Western Manichaeism (L.J.R. Ort, Mani. A religio-bistorical description of bis personality [Leiden 19671, p.94). But W. Sundermann (W. SUNDERMANN, Der Paraklet in der Ostmanicháischen Uberlieferung: P.BrYDER [ed.], Manichaean Studies, p.201-212) has shown that it is not lacking in the Eastern Manichean sources.

Leaving aside Manes' personal experience that led him to consider himself the Parasite, the Manichaeans had their reasons for admitting him as such. The most explicit reasoning has been left to us by the Manichean doctor Félix. The starting point is the pious promise to send the Holy Spirit Paraclete who will introduce the full truth; Given that no one has provided global knowledge like Manés has done, who has taught things related to the three times, the making of the world, etc., he concludes that Manés is necessarily the Paraclete. "Since we have not heard anything of this in Paul or in the writings of other apostles, we believe that Manes in person is the Paraclete" (C. Fel. 12.6.9). Manés is above Paul because the former has provided full knowledge, while the latter speaks only of partial knowledge (1 Cor 13,9-10) (C. Fel. 19; cf. F. DÉcREr, Aspects, p.293-294). He has taught the naked, unveiled and complete truth (XV 5). Manes is a Paraclete precisely in that he is above all an enlightener, who had to provide the full gnosis that brings salvation, according to Jn 14:26 and 16:13, although the listener does not forget his role as defense lawyer, particularly in the trial (Epist. Secund. [31).

The specific problem consists of knowing how Manes' relationship with the Paraclete is to be understood, whether of identity with him personally or simple presence, identifying in this case with his "Twin" (syzygos), since the texts point in both directions. When expressing the beliefs of the Manichaeans, Augustine is rich in nuances that range from the simple function of mediation for their sending, to identity without more, or simple dwelling (cf. the texts in F. Dcrer, L'afrique L, p.279-281). One of the most significant texts is found precisely in our work where Augustine presents two possibilities: "Relying on this promise (to send the Paraclete), they affirm that Manés is that Paraclete or that he was in him" (XII 17).

Which of the two possibilities is true? The sources are not univocal and scholars have expressed themselves differently. For some, the various formulas respond to two successive stages in the same understanding that Manés had of himself: moving from the idea of ​​the Holy Spirit dwelling in him to that of identification with him. It is HJ's opinion. Polotsky (Ein Manifund in Agypten, and H.H. Schraeder (review of the previous work in Gnomon 9 [1933] 351-352), among others. Others, on the contrary, believe that Manes only considered his "Twin" as the Paraclete predicted by Jesus, his Church being the one who later identified him with the Paraclete. This is what P. Nagel thinks (Der Parakletenanspruch des Mani (Kepb. 1,14,7-11) and die Altsyrische Evangelienúbersetzung: Mitteilung der Agyptischen Sammlung 8 [1975] 303, n.7) and K. Rudolph (Die Bedeutung der Kólner Mani Kodex fir die Manichtismusforscbung: Mélanges d'Histoire des Religions offerts 4 H.C. Puech [Paris 1974] 478-480). Both positions are supported by the first Kephalaion "On the Coming of the Apostle", in particular 1,14,32;

In any case, the text of Augustine cited above always leaves the door open to the other possibility. Text that, according to L. In fact, this author maintains that there is no contradiction between the various sources, if the Gnostic concept of the "Twin" is considered. For Augustine, presenting himself as the Paraclete promised by him was equivalent to uniting his person with the Holy Spirit. According to him, Manés had established between his person and the Paraclete (third Person of the Trinity), the same as in Christ between the second person of the Trinity and the son of Mary (C. epist. fund. 6). But for this to be true, a condition would be required to be met that in fact is not met, namely, that they participate in the same Trinitarian theology. Cf. on all this recently F. Decker, Mani «l'autre Paraclet»: Augustinianam 32 (1992) 105-118.

[19] The diabolical privilege (X 3).—One of the aspects of Manichaeism on which our work provides the greatest wealth of data is, without a doubt, that of exegesis. Faustus appears above all as a skilled exegete, as well as an extraordinary expert on the Scriptures, both the Old and New Testaments; also aware of the exegesis of his opponents, the Catholics. Augustine, for his part, contributes with quite a bit of information to make us better aware of this aspect of Manichean thought.

But exegesis is exercised on a text. In a fight to appropriate "Christian" ownership, this text could not be other than the Scriptures, a point of meeting and friction at the same time, so there was coincidence and disagreement between the Catholic Church and the Manichean "Congregation." At this moment we are mainly concerned with the discrepancy. The question to be resolved was twofold: which Ebros are truly apostolic and whether everything they contain is apostolic or from the Lord. What books can be considered Christian Scriptures? Here is the first discrepancy, which is fundamental. The Manichaeans reject the Old Testament outright. As for the New, they accept it formally, but not in all its materiality. Not all of their content is considered authentic. We will first see which parts they expunge; then the criteria followed, as they appear in the mouths of their spokespersons, particularly Fausto.

Directly from Faust we know that they considered Mt 1,1ss (11 1; HI 1) as interpolations; Mt 5,17 (XVII 1-3); Mt 8,11 (XXXII 1-3); Jn 5,46 (XVI 1-3); Rom 1,3 (XI 1; XXI 1); 1 Tim 4:1-4 (XXX 1-4); Tit 1,151-16) (XXXI 1-3). From information from Augustine we know that they considered Mt 19,3-9 as interpolations (C. Adíman. 3, [2]); 1 Tim 1,15 (C. Adiman. 28 [17); Rom 8:36 (De moribus 19:14), etc. In view of these data, although they are incomplete, Augustine's statement in his letter may seem excessive.

Supplementary Notes 791 to Jerome that the Manichaeans maintain that most of the Holy Scriptures are falsified (Epist. 82,2,6). But it no longer seems that way if we take into account that Augustine also has in mind his rejection of the entire Old Testament as well as the book of the Acts of the Apostles. This last fact is widely attested by Augustine (XIX 31; C. Adiman. 17 [5]; C. eptst. fund. 5), who also gives the reason: to maintain the truth of his belief that Manes is the Paraclete. If the authenticity and truth of the Acts were maintained, the truth of the coming of the Paraclete promised by Jesus would have to be maintained, and then their claim that this promise was fulfilled in Manes, the last divine envoy, who revealed all the secrets, would fall to the ground.

The Scriptures only have authority and the maximum authority once they have been purged of everything foreign to them (C. Fortun. 19-20). Here is the difficulty: knowing what is your own and what is foreign. The Lord warned us that the enemy sows tares in the field at night (Mt 13:28) (XVII 3). That enemy identifies with people infected with Judaism. The prince of darkness has used them to spread his error. The ES of the Catholics have interspersed many things in the Lord's speeches that, despite bearing his name, do not conform to faith in him (XXXII 3). Unlike Manes, Jesus did not personally write his doctrine; There have been others who have written the gospels after the death of the apostles based on vague rumors, without agreeing on them among themselves and overflowing with Judaism (XXXIII 3). The evangelists, in short, have not been eyewitnesses (VII 1).

It is necessary, therefore, to subject all texts to criticism before using them (XVI 8). There is nothing strange, therefore, in taking from the New Testament what is pure in it and suitable for salvation, leaving aside what others have fraudulently introduced (XXXI 1).

Fausto has given us a good example of this way of proceeding. It is not limited to stating that certain evangelical or Pauline texts have been interpolated. It also gives us the principles of discernment. The last principle, not made explicit, is external to the text examined: Manes was the last of the Prophets (cf. supplementary note 28), he is the Paraclete promised by Jesus, who therefore introduces all truth and clarifies all enigmas (cf. supplementary note 18). In practice, give the ultimate criterion of truth. What is not agreed with him must be considered false; it cannot have been said by Jesus or written by the Apostle; Consequently, the text in question must be considered as interpo-

Already explicitly, the ultimate criterion is the Manichean faith itself, that is, a dogmatic criterion. Faust says it without hesitation: «(We accept) the things that build our faith and bring glory to Christ the Lord and his omnipotent Father God; We reject the rest to the extent that they do not conform to the divine Majesties or our faith” (XXXII 2). In other words: «From the New Testament we only accept what brings honor and praise to the Son of the Majesty, or what we notice to have been said by himself or by his apostles; but, now perfect and faithful, we leave aside the other things that were said in a simple and ignorant manner by rude people, or were launched indirectly and maliciously by enemies, or were stated imprudently by writers, but then passed on to posterity” (XXXII 7). And one way to save the glory of Jesus is to save his truthfulness. Thus Faustus, before Jn 5:46, shows the anguish he suffers, faced with the alternative of considering said passage as False, and therefore interpolated, or accusing Jesus of being a liar. Since the latter would be impious, he has no choice but to accept the other assumption (XVI 2).

As the glory of Jesus must be saved, the laws of nature must also be safeguarded: if the content of a text goes against them, it must be rejected (XXVI 1).

But in order to apply the previous criteria, it is necessary to know its authentic interpretation. To determine it, Faustus recommends considering the context (XIX 3) and comparing some things with others (XXXII 3).

Authentic Scriptures cannot be contradicted (C. Fortun. 19). But in fact contradiction can and does appear between two or more scriptural texts. It is obvious that both cannot be true. The consequence will be, again, that the text that does not conform to the truth has been interpolated. The difficulty here may be in showing that contradiction. Fausto is particularly skilled at making it stand out. Sometimes he opposes various evangelical passages in order to choose between them to his liking; Others show internal contradictions within the same author. It is enough to see the contradictions that stand out between Mt and Lc on the one hand and between these two evangelists and Mc and Jn on the other, in order to reject the genealogies (HI 1), for being the work of a forger. Any internal contradiction in an author's writings leads to the conclusion that the text has been interpolated. A clear example of this is seen in Paul, specifically in Rom 1:3, which contradicts 2 Cor 5:16-17). Only if one admits the possibility that it is a change of opinion produced over time (XI 1) can one deny that it is the work of an interpolator.

Other times Faustus prefers a kind of ad honinem argument: the Manichaeans do with the Testament of the Son (=New) the same as the Catholics do with the Testament of the Father (Old): although they claim to accept it, they reject from it what seems good to them (XXXII 2.5.7). Knowing that texts such as 1 Tim 4:1-4 or Tit 1:15 attack the fundamental principles of Manichaeism, they have no choice but to consider them as interpolated. To do this, with remarkable skill. Faust tries to demonstrate that to claim its authenticity would go against the beliefs and life of the Catholics themselves: such texts contradict the teachings of Lev 11:3-8, of Christ, of Paul and, in a particular way, the behavior of the most select Catholics themselves (XXX 3-4). Hence Faustus's warning: before accusing, be careful lest the accusation turn against you (XXXI 3). In short, Catholics must admit that these are interpolated texts if they do not want to be bound by the consequences that would arise. Cf. FAITH. DÉcRET, Aspects, p.152-154; 174-182; Ip., Tentilisation, p.44-51.
Augustine's reply to this procedure that he calls "diabolical privilege" can be seen in our general introduction (OCSA XXX, BAC 487, p.41-42; 112-117).

[20] Sin and its author (XII 13).—Faust never mentions sin. But by maintaining that man must be reborn to unity, putting off the old man and converting to faith (XXIV 1), he recognizes that man is in a sinful, torn situation. Sin is connatural to the soul in a carnal situation.
For his part, Augustine refers twice to the Manichaean conception of sin. Both in XII 13 and XXII 22 he points out that the Manichaeans attribute it to the race of darkness, not to man's own will.
It is worth asking if what Augustine stated is true or, at least, if it is the entire truth.

In this regard, it is appropriate to point out that texts from the founder, formulations from followers and the praxis of the sect point in another direction. The Charter of the Foundation, in its very entry, speaks of the "healthy words that

Additional notes 793 flow from the living and perennial source", to later add that whoever hears them, believes them and fulfills them will not be subject to death and will enjoy eternal and glorious life (C. epist. fund. 11,12). Another text, probably from the same Letter, speaks of souls who "tolerated a departure from their former luminous nature and became enemies of the holy light" (XXI 22).

In the mouth of the priest Fortunatus we find these words: «If there is sin in the soul, it only occurs after having been warned by our Savior and having received his sound doctrine; after having separated from the contrary and enemy race and having adorned itself with purer realities. Words that are supported by the text of Jn 15:22: 5If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have had no sin; But now that I have come and spoken to them and they did not want to believe me, they will not have forgiveness for their sin (C. Fortun. 21). The listener Secundino, for his part, writes: «If (the soul), after knowing itself, gives its consent to evil and does not arm itself against the enemy, it has sinned of its own will. If he is again ashamed of having erred, he will find the author of mercies ready; She is not punished for having sinned, but for not having felt pain for sin" (Secondary Epist. (21).

text from Fortunato quoted above, these words follow: "From here it appears that penance has been opportunely given after the coming of the Savior and after having granted that knowledge, by which the soul, as if washed in the divine fountain of stains and vices..., can become present again in the kingdom of God from which it came." Indeed, in the practice of the sect, penance occupied an important place. The confession of sins was obligatory for all, "hearers" and "elect" (cf. W. Ban6, Manichaische Laien-Beichtspiegel: Le Muséon 36 [1923] 137-242; J.P. ASMUSSEN, Xuatvanift, Studies in Manichaeism (Copenhagen, 19651). One of the meanings of its most important festival, that of Bema, was to be the day of forgiveness of sins (cf. complementary note 27).

From these data the following is unequivocally deduced: first, that the soul can sin of its own will; second, that this sin can only take place once one has received the illumination of gnosis, and involves personal consent; third, that this sin has the doors of forgiveness open, as long as pain precedes it. Which combines perfectly with the existence in everyone of another "necessary" sin before said enlightenment, which both Fortunatus and Secundino speak of (1b.). In other words: there are two kinds of sin: one involuntary, always prior to the reception of Gnostic knowledge, and another voluntary, after it. Ultimately, nothing new compared to the same Catholic teaching: every man is born with original sin, involuntary, in that it was not his direct and personal decision, and then, once he knows the law of God, he can and does transgress it voluntarily.

Is Augustine's information false, then? No. Due to personal interests, he leaves aside the second moment or stage and deals only with the first. And this is where the difference between the Catholic and Manichean conception lies. While for Catholics, the "original" sin was voluntary, for two Manichaeans it was not. Adam, the author of sin that was then passed on to others, sinned of his own free will; In the Manichean doctrine, this "original" sin is a direct consequence of the dualism of substances, without any human will that causes it. According to Catholic doctrine, both original sin and other sins originate in human will. In the first case, in the will of Adam who represented all his descendants; in the second, in the will of each specific person. According to the Manichean doctrine, the first is involuntary, Psecond voluntary.

One can even add more: the adjective "natural" does not have the same meaning in the Manichean conception as in the Augustinian conception. [21] The allegorical interpretation (XII 40).—Regarding the inter; allegorical challenge, in his reply to Faust Augustine follows a double procedure: Negative the Catholic practice referred to Scripture, particularly the Old Testament, and delegitimize its use by the Manichaeans, referring to their own writings.

The defense in Catholic exegesis was not difficult for him. On the one hand it had the teaching of the Apostle, on the other hand it had the practice of Jews and pagans. Texts such as 1 Cor 10,6.11 gave apostolic coverage to such a procedure, at the level of principles, and Gal 4,22ff at the level of specific cases that serve as an example (XII 37). From there he concludes that only

Whoever comes to read it, perverse spirit, may doubt that the facts and words of the Old Testament contain other meanings that go beyond the purely literal. Such praxis was not foreign to the Jews, as proven by the work of Philo of Alexandria. It is also a significant case because it shows how one can err when one deviates from the only valid criterion of interpretation, which is the reference to Christ and his Church (XII 39). Finally, not even pagans reproach Catholics for anything in this regard. They interpret their own fables by referring them to certain natural or divine reasons (XII 40), to the nature of things Or to the customs of men (XX 9 with abundant examples).

But the case of Manés' writings is different. In his polemic Augustine interprets them in their most literal sense. Faced with the accusation of using double measurement, one for the Old Testament and the other for the books of Manes, he gives the reasons for his actions, which are none other than two points of the Manichaean teaching regarding Manes: the first is that he is the last prophet, after whom no one else will come (cÉ. complementary note 28); Secondly, he taught the truth in its entirety and without veils, with complete clarity (c£, the various texts in which Augustine refers to that clarity in F. Dicrer, L'Afrique, p.249-251). If Paul speaks of his knowledge being partial and enigmatic (1 Cor 13:9-11), Manés came to bring that full knowledge for which Paul longs (XV' 6; C. Fel. 19).

The allegorical interpretation, as a gateway to whatever absurd, irrational or immoral is found in them, was closed to the writings of Manés. It cannot be admitted that what is narrated in them could have spiritual symbolism (meystica significatione). Augustine sticks to the same words as the Manichaeans. In fact, he says to Fausto: «You usually praise Manés over

all because, leaving aside all symbolic cover, it presents you with the naked and faithful truth” (XV 5). The Manichaeans themselves affirmed that Manes, knowing that no one would come after him, had dispensed with all allegorical circumlocution, something that the prophets who had preceded him had not done. These did act or speak in figures, De: in the assurance that Manés, who would arrive later, would clarify them all (XV 6). His function as Paraclete, who introduces into all truth (cÉ. note with
Supplementary notes 795 supplementary 18), entails deciphering every enigma or every figure, contributing to full revelation.

A few years earlier Augustine had expressed the same thing with identical clarity: «(The Manichaeans) attribute to their founder, with almost exclusive and exalted praise, that to him, who was to come last, were reserved, so that he could decipher and discover them, the divine mysteries that the ancients left in their books in a figurative sense. Consequently, they affirm that no other doctor sent by God will come after him, since he, Manes, did not express anything through symbols and allegories, rather it was he who revealed those of the ancients and showed what was his in a clear and manifest way" (C. epist. fund. 23,25). Neither in fact nor in law did anyone come or could come after Manés.

Augustine's words do not fit into a scholarly discussion of allegorical interpretation as such. The point he intends to get to is to show that these stories are nothing more than creations of the imagination. The logic of his speech is this: Such stories cannot be interpreted either in their own sense, since the result is absurd or immoral, or in an allegorical sense from the same Manichean principles. Therefore it is a creation of the imagination (XX 9.19).

Such was the reasoning of Augustine, accustomed to interpreting the Scriptures. The Manichaeans, on the other hand, judging by Felix's words, did not follow that path. Scripture interprets itself (C. Fel. 1 17.19). In any case, the debates held by Augustine with Manichaeans show how they did not enter into interpretations, neither literal nor allegorical, of those texts of Manes; Even more they considered it a sin (C. Fel. 1 19). The aspects that Augustine most insistently criticizes are those that they most overlook.

Although he absolutely rejects the allegorical interpretation given by Catholics to the Old Testament, in other writings Faustus seems to admit the existence of an allegorical interpretation. Commenting on the vision of Peter in Joppa related by the Acts of the Apostles 10,13-15, a book that they did not adonite ((c£. complementary note 19), he refers to an allegorical interpretation against the interpretation offered by Catholics (XXXI 3).

(23] The three times of the Manichean myth (XUL 6).—Together with the doctrine of the two roots or principles, the teaching of the three times summarized the entire Manichean catechesis (W. BANG, Manichaische, p.157; E. CHAVANNESP. PeLu1Or, Un traité manichéen, p.114-116). They are the following: the beginning, the middle and the end, or previous time, middle and Later, neither Fortunatus nor Faustus makes mention of them, Felix does (C. Fel. 16; UL 7), as well as Augustine (XII 6; XXVIII 5).

The entire drama described by the Manichean myth unfolds in three acts or times. The first (previous time), prehistoric, the second (middle), historical; the third (later), posthistorical. The first is prior to the existence of the world: only the two principles existed, the kingdoms of Light and Darkness, antagonistic by nature, but in tranquility and repose. In the second, the kingdom of Darkness invades the kingdom of Light, the mixture between one and the other occurs, leaving the Light imprisoned in the clutches of Darkness; God manufactures the world to achieve the separation of light which is equivalent to its liberation through certain processes. In the third the original separation is reestablished. Defined from the relationship between the two principles, they can be spoken of as "before, during and after
'a mix between the two.' Such is the division that appears in Eastern texts (cf. H.C. Puch, Le manicháisme, p.157-159, n. 284).

However, other sources, such as Kephalaion 17, dispense with the two stages of separation between both principles, and introduce the three times within the average time, that of mixture, of the previous classification. In accordance with clio, the first time begins with the struggle between both principles and concludes with the liberation of the First Man (cf. complementary note 3), the second coincides with the creation of the world and the third with the time of salvation. This classification is what emerges from the Augustinian texts (XIII 6; XXVI. 5; cf. De natura boni 43, C. Fel. II 7.13: crudeliter neiscendamz, turpiter purgandam, inique damnandam; also C. Fel. [24] The children of the Living Spirit (XV 5.6).—Several times in our work we find mentioned a series of "hypostasis" of the Manichean myth, which the Bishop of Hippo does not designate as "Sons of the Living Spirit" according to the title of this note and as is the case, for example, in Bar Khonai (A. Apam, Texte, p.19; A. BOHLIG, Die Gnosis HI, p.105). "Hypostasis" that are silenced by Augustine himself in his other writings, including his catalog of heresies, which is somewhat surprising, as well as by his Manichean opponents. The latter is less surprising, given the line of action they always followed, that is, making the minimum reference to the myth, perhaps as a means to avoid ridicule, and paying attention above all to attracting followers, to which such aspects did not contribute much.

The "hypostasis" are, in the order in which Augustine cites them in his only complete mention (XV 6), the following: the Support of Splendor (Splenditenens in Latin, Doxokrator and Pheggokatokhos in Greek; cf. A. BOHLIG, Die Gnosis UI, p.56), The King of Honor, Adamante, The King of glory, and Atlas. The remaining times (XV 5; XX 9; XXIT 12; XXXII 19) he mentions only two of them: the Support of Splendor and Atlas, with one exception in which he adds the King of Honor (XXII 11). But only in one text are they the only ones to be named (XV 5). In XV 6 they appear preceded by an army of gods (cf. supplementary note 25), in XXXII 19 of the eight lands and ten heavens (cf. supplementary note 6); in XX 9 of the Mighty Spirit (Augustinian version of the Living Spirit from other sources); in XX 12 of the First Man and the Mighty Spirit, and in XX 11 they are followed by these last "hypostasis", in reverse order.

The Augustinian presentation does not allow us to capture the succession and order of all these "hypostasis", which belong to different levels of development of the myth. And it is understandable. His work is not an exhibition of himself as such, but rather a replica work. The elements of the myth do not enter by themselves, but as a function of other interests, always controversial and never "scientific." Hence the way to consider them.

In fact the First Man belongs to the first Triad of which he occupies the last place: Father, Mother of life and First Man (complementary note 3); the Powerful Spirit in turn occupies the last of the second: Friend of the lights, great Architect and Powerful Spirit (cf. complementary note 6). Now, the five "hypostasis" mentioned above are children of this Thymus. As the Mighty Spirit is the one who has manufactured the world, these his children, evoked by him, have functions in relation to said world, which Augustine refers to in the places referred to: in XV 5, XX 9, XXXII 19 for the Support of Splendor and Atlas, and in XV 6 for everyone. For the different names by which they are designated in the different sources, cf. M. TARDIEU, Le manicheisme, p.105-106 andA. BOHBLIG, Die Gnosis II, p.62.

BANG, Manicháische, p.155) forgiveness is asked for if "considering the devil and spirits as gods, living beings have been offered to them as an offering." This text is a testimony in favor of Faustus in the controversy held with Augustine over whether the Manichaeans were ditheists or not.
But Augustine was not alone in maintaining this, not admitting, which is impossible, that Faustus had written his work against Augustine himself. The Manichaean Bishop

He issues chapters XX 1-4 and more specifically XXI 1 to defend himself against said accusation. So it was something real. Accusation that was supported on two pillars: one, the very way of speaking of the Manichaeans; another, a principle of logic.

As for the first, as if anticipating the reply that he would later bequeath to him from Augustine and that could come to him from many others, Faust himself recognizes that sometimes Alann God to nature contrary to that of light. But he adds that they do so not from their own convictions but to conform to the way of speaking of their opponents, just as Paul does in 2 Cor 4:4 (XXI 1). Which leaves the impression that it is something purely occasional. Augustine, for his part, points out that it was a common way of speaking (solemus) in the discussions (XXI 2), at the same time that, putting on the grammarian's livery, he attempts to remove Paul's support from his opponent, giving another different interpretation of said text, in the sense that the God who blinds the minds of the unbelievers is the only God, without introducing another. Modern exegesis takes away Augustine's reason and gives it to Faustus.

Leaving aside this, which for Faustus is nothing more than something anecdotal, the Manichean bishop relies on names: "It is true that we confess two principles, but we call one of them God and the other Hyle, or, to use a common and frequent expression, demon" (XXI 1). To which Augustine, and without Jada others like him would, responds that it is not about names, but realities: "If you ask him what Hyle calls, you will hear him describe exactly another God" (XXI 3). In this context, he examines the concept of Hyle typical of Greek philosophy and that maintained by the Manichaeans. The conclusion reached is twofold: the ignorance, for themselves, of the Manichaeans about said philosophical concept. and that they assign to said Hyle what properly corresponds to God (XX 14; XXI 3). Therefore, regardless of how they designate both principles, given what they attribute to them, logically, we must conclude that they admit two gods.

But «what did Manés have to do with logic? He was a poet and must be judged as such” (W. BANG, Manicbáische, p.204). In any case, it is a logic that reasons from "Catholic" assumptions, from the monarchy that Faust speaks of, not from dualism. Catholic logic only to a certain point. In fact, to reach such a conclusion they must focus on only one aspect of their conception of God: him as the author of everything that exists. Admitted that Hyle is the ultimate origin of bodies, it is assimilated to God. But if two debaters had paid attention to another quality of God, his goodness, for example, they would have had more difficulty in assimilating the Principle of evil to God.
On the other hand, in other passages, having already forgotten this specific point of the controversy, he has no qualms about speaking of your God, in the singular (XXI 22).

This is also where “Catholic” logic comes in. Augustine's criticism is directed above all against the Manichaean pantheon, to use an expression by M. [26] Immorality of the Manichean God (XV 7).—In the polemic against his former coreligionists, Augustine usually exploits everything he finds incongruous (e.g., that God saw the need to fight) or immoral in the Manichean myth. On the moral aspect, Augustine usually brings together three accusations, corresponding to the three periods of the myth, against the Manichaean god: cruelty, clumsiness and injustice, since God sent his nature to a cruel mixture, to a clumsy purification and to an unjust condemnation (crudeliter miscendam, turpiter purgandam, inique damnandam: De natura boni 43; C. Fel, 17.13). Here we limit ourselves to the accusation of clumsiness, by the method that God uses to purify the part of light imprisoned in the princes of darkness. It is one of the themes used both in the hand-in-hand controversy (XV 7; XX 6.8; C. Fel. 11 7.13.22) and in the simple doctrinal exposition (De haeres. 46,8-10 and De natura boni 44). It is in De natura boni where he comments on it more fully, literally quoting an extensive text from the seventh book of Manés' work El Tesoro.

The episode narrated is certainly unusual. To such an extent that L de Beausobre considered that Augustine was the victim of a poorly translated or corrupted text, without providing any evidence other than the obscenity it contained. In favor of its authenticity, on the contrary, is the fact that the Manichaean doctor Felix never objects to anything when Augustine reproaches him three times (cf. F. Décrer, L'Afrique U, p.92, p.35). On the other hand, it is not only Augustine who informs us about this. With less abundance of data,
But with identical content, Bar Khonai also refers to it (A. ADAM, ente, p.20; A. BónLiG, Die Gnosís UI, p.106). We also find it in Commonitorium 5 (CSEL 25, 980).

In summary it boils down to the following: When the world was created, some of the princes of darkness, males and females, were nailed to the heavenly vaults. As they had devoured the elements of the First Man (cf. supplementary note 5) they had within them particles of light, which the

Father intended to release. In line with the entire system, said light was concentrated in the semen of the princes. In order to obtain said liberation, God, who dwells in the celestial ships (cf. complementary speck 15), transforms his powers (virtutes), identical to himself, into young men who display themselves naked in the opposite sex to that of the prince of darkness before whom they make such a display: as males before females and as females before males. Their figures, extremely beautiful, excite their concupiscence and cause the ejaculation of semen, which contains most of the divine substance they possess. Thus, through this stratagem, using the same concupiscence, the vital substance is released, that is, the divine part, which, depending on the level of purification, goes to the divine ships or falls to the earth. Bar Khonai puts it this way: “Sin fell on the earth, half on the wet and half on the dry. The half fallen on the damp became a horrible Beast, similar to the king of darkness. The Adamant of light was sent against her, he entered into combat with her, defeated her, turned her back and with a spear pierced her heart... As for the half that had fallen on the dry ground, it sprouted into five trees» (A. Anam, Texte, p.21; A. BómLIG, Die Gnosis UÍ, p.107). There we have the origin of trees and animals (cf. supplementary note 16).

To Faustus who, because he is part of the primitive revelation (cf. complementary note 28), has just defended the validity of some precepts of the Decalogue, despite being contained in the Old Testament, Augustine replies by showing how fidelity to the teachings of the sect includes the violation of almost all of them. There is one that does not: the precept of not desiring one's neighbor's wife. But that is nothing compared to other derivations: "If it is unlawful to desire another's wife, consider how it is unlawful to propose another's wife as an object of desire, and remember that your gods were exhibited... to excite ardent desire" (XV 7). To better serve his plans, Augustine takes the story literally, acting in the same way as the Manichean polemicists act with the Old Testament. From then on, the behavior of the Bishop of Hippo does not stop at accusing God of being dishonest and clumsy; He goes on to accuse him of being a criminal in that such behavior causes the death of other souls, which is why it encourages him to behave in certain ways. It is the difference with respect to the other accusations. The part of the myth that gives rise to the accusation of "cruelty and injustice is tolerable in that, deep down, it is rather an object of laughter or tears, while this other part is intolerable because it is criminal (XX 6). [271 The Feast of the Bema (XVII 5).—In his only reference in Contra Faustum to the main Manichaean liturgical festival, the Feast of the Bema, Augustine only gives us one piece of information: that it was celebrated in the month of March (XVII 5). More abundant, however, he offers us in his refutation of the Letter of the Foundation (C. epist. and. 8). In this text he informs us about different aspects of the celebration, in many ways modeled on that of the Christian Easter: the sense of celebration, the date of celebration, the spiritual preparation, the reason for celebrating and the external framework.

Augustine's words make very clear the festive feeling, of "great solemnity", that overwhelmed the participants. It was an “intensely desired” holiday, somewhat out of a desire to rival Catholic Easter. Contrary to what happened in the celebration of Christ's Easter by the Manichaeans themselves, the "attendance was extraordinary and filled with fervor." In keeping with the solemnity of the moment, everyone, "elect" and "listeners", gathered around the Founder.

The festival had an intense religious preparation, consisting of "vigils", "longer fasts even for the "listeners"". Fasts that long prepared the festival: «From the Enal of autumn until the end of winter, the Manichaeans of all ranks observed a series of three double fasts in memory of their holy martyrs, followed by a quarter of a month long in memory of their Founder, with which the year was closed. The end of the fast was marked by the celebration of Bema. Just as the beginning of the great annual fast (February 8) corresponded to the entry of Manés into prison and torture, the end of the fast corresponded to the supposed date of his liberation and ascension to heaven (March 8)» (M. TarDIEU, Le Manicheisme, p.91-92; cf. also A. BÓHLIG, Die Gnosis II, p.42). The night preceding the celebration was spent in prayer and singing.

The festival, held annually, was celebrated at the beginning of March, around the spring equinox, again in certain concurrence with the Christian Easter and coinciding with the anniversary of the death of Manés.

This death was indeed one of the aspects, in Africa perhaps the main one, that was remembered and celebrated, judging by the words of Augustine: "On the day when Manes was killed." In their symbolic-mystical language, the Manichaeans designated this death as "crucifixion", a designation that bears the seal of Pauline theology, since Manes did not die through that torture. The greater importance given to the celebration of the death of Manés than to that of Jesus, was due, comments Augustine, to the fact that the death of Manes had been real while that of Christ had only been apparent. But something else was celebrated: with the Passion of Manés the missionary force of gnosis and the forgiveness of sins that announced the final judgment were also celebrated (J. Rres, La féte de Béma dans l'Eglise de Mani: Revue des Études Augustiniennes 22 [1976] 221-229; Ib., La gnose dans les textes liturgiques manichéens coptes: Le origini dello gnosticismo, Messina 1966, 615.618).

Augustine does not tell us about the development of the liturgy of the feast. According to M. Tardieu's reconstruction, it would consist of the following moments: Reading of the passion of Manés, prayers of intercession and praise, solemn celebration of the Gospel of Manés, penitential rite, reading of the Letter of the seal, singing of the cxulet sacred banquet and song of thanksgiving (b., p.92-93).

The external framework was appropriate to signify the festive nature and the very meaning of what was celebrated. "A platform (cabbage) with five steps was erected like a court, adorned with precious carpets, placed in view of all and offered for adoration", surrounded by the gifts of fruits and pastries and roses brought by the "listeners." On the platform, a symbol of both an ibunal and a chair, an allusion to the function of Manés as a judge and/or lawyer (cf. Epist. Secund. (3) and as a revealer of gnosis, presided over an image of Manés himself (on the meaning of Bema, cf. J. Rres, La féte de Béma, p.219-221; on other interpretations of said platform, b. p.218-219). On the five steps are the works of Manés, which symbolized the five degrees in the hierarchy of the Manichean Church (thus F. DÉCRET, Mani, p.118) or the five greatnesses of the

[28] The prophets of truth (XIX 3).—Twice Faustus mentions, valuing them positively, characters from the Old Testament. The first time he expressly cites Seth and Enoch as righteous men by whom those precepts of the Decalogue of universal validity, not only for the Jews, were promulgated in ancient times. In fact, the angels handed them over to them (XIX 3). In the second, the Manichean bishop reproaches Catholics for limiting themselves to speaking of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, overlooking other righteous people who existed before, such as Enoch, Noah and Shem, and others like them (XXV 1). From what we will say below, among those other "similar ones" that Faustus refers to are Adam and Enos. At first glance, Faust's positive assessment of characters from the Old Testament is surprising, despite his absolute rejection of it. But this strangeness is lessened when it is noted that these characters are alien to the Jewish religion, because they predate Abraham, as Faust himself points out.

The revelation of God did not appear as new with Manes or even with the historical Jesus. These are nothing more than links in a long chain of "apostles" or "prophets" through whom the revelation of truth has come to men, "wisdom and works", in our specific case of the moral truths contained in part of the precepts of the Decalogue. In all of them Jesus acts (cf. R. MErKELBACH, Mani und sein Religionssystem, p.29; E. RosE, Die manicháische Christologie, 11758).

This chain begins with Adam and ends in Manes, "the seal of the prophets" (title questioned by G.STROUSA, "Seal of the Prophets". The Nature of a Manichaean Metaphor: Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam 7 [1986] 61-74). Different sources give us lists, not all equally complete, but coinciding in their terms, with some exceptions. We already have one in the CMC. To justify the message of Manes and his revelations, it is shown that it is not something new and exceptional, but rather that it is inserted in the history of revelations, witnessed by the

Pocalipsis of Adam (CMC 48.6-50.7), Seth (el) (50.8-52.7), Enos (52.855.9), Shem (55.10-58.5), Enoch (58.6-60.12), Paul (60.13-62.9). In As-Sahrastani's work on the Manichaeans he says of them: "Regarding the Law

The Prophets believe that the first whom God sent with knowledge and wisdom was Adam, the Father of the human race, after him he sent Seth; then Noah and Abraham; then he sent Buddha to India, Zarathushtra to Persia, and to the land of the Greeks and the West Christ, the Word of God and his Spirit, and after Christ to Paul. Finally came the seal of the prophets (Manes) to the land of the Arabs" (A. BOHLIG, Die Gnosis,

Supplementary notes 803 II 155). The first chapter of the Saburagan, transmitted by Al-Biruni (Chronology of the ancient peoples) once again integrates Manés into the series of the great founders of religions, reserving for him, the envoy of the true God, the land of Babel (4. Anam, Texte, p. 5-6). They are not the only texts. Significant is the first Kephalaton. Although in poor condition, it mentions Setel, Adam's firstborn, Enos, Enoch, Shem, Buddha, Zarathustra, Jesus (I 12,9-14,3). Another list appears in the Coptic Psalter, including Shetel, Enos, Noah, Shem, Jesus and apostles (Psalm 142,3ff; cf. also Homily 68,15ff; Seven Chapters 2,31-32 [S.N.C. Lrzu, An Early Byzantine Formula, p. 176.1921). Other data can be seen in M. Tardieu, Le manicháisme, p.19-27 andA. HeNrICHS-L. KOENEN, Ein Griechischer Mani Kodex: ZEP 5 [1970] 107, no. 21). St. Ephrem includes among the Manichaean apostles Hermes Trismegistus in Egypt and Plato among the Greeks (C.W'MrTcHELL, $. Ephraim's Prose Refutations A Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan, 2 vol. [London 1912 and 1921], Il, p.XCVIM) and an allusion to it is found in Faust (XUT 1).

From this list of apostles (Keph. 1,12,9ff) or prophets of truth (CMC 62,13-14; Keph. 59,150,25) the patriarchs, the legislator and the prophets of Judaism are excluded because they considered it a corruption of the primitive and true religion. Faustus speaks of those "before Abraham", because he was the father of Judaism (Jn 8,33.37.39). That is why the mention in the text of As-Sahrastani, if it is authentic, of Abraham, so reviled by Faust (XXII 5), is surprising.

On the other hand, placing Manés in the series of founders of the great religions means, on the one hand, that God has continued to reveal wisdom and science to men in all times and places, and on the other, that Manés considers that he contributes plenitude to all the religions of the world (cf. N. A. PEDERSEN, Early, p.166-169: The Comtinuous Revelation: The Succession of the Apostles. The historical Jesus).

Although all are bearers of divine revelation, some of these prophets receive greater consideration. An example is Seth, the son of Adam whom the Manichaeans, like the Mandeans, call Setel, where the suffix -el is intended to indicate his somewhat divine character. Furthermore, the highest category within the Manichaean religion, that is, that of the "elect" (i.e., that of chastity) is symbolically associated with Seth, while that of the "hearers" (resp. that of continence) with Adam (B. A. Pearson, The Figure of Seth in Manichaean Literature: P.BRYDER (Ed.), Manichaean Studies, p.147-155, esp. 152).
The idea of continuous revelation is considered by scholars to have influenced Manes of the Elcasaites (cf. N.A. Pearson, Early, p.180).

[29] Manichaean Trinity (XX 2).—Augustine describes his fall into Manichaeism with these words: «Thus I came upon some men... in whose mouth there is... a viscous garter made with the syllables of your name, that of our Lord Jesus Christ and that of our Paraclete and Comforter, the Holy Spirit. These names did not depart from their mouths, but only in the sound and noise of the mouth, since otherwise their heart was truly empty” (Conf. II 6,10). Words that include a confirmation: the Manichaeans admitted a "Trinity", and a judgment: that Trinity is only nominal.

It is not difficult to understand the negative judgment of the Bishop of Hippo and it does not require us to dwell on it. The Manichaean "Trinity" is not the Catholic one; lacks truth. It is more interesting to know how the Manichaeans conceived this "Trinity."

These "forms" do not participate in the "inaccessible" light that is proper to the nature of the Father; but they do participate in the divine substance, in the same way as other souls, but they do not have the divine nature. Son and Holy Spirit mean emanations, not personalized, of the Father's action to oppose the root of evil. [30] The Manichaean "Eucharist" (XX 2).—If one keeps one's mind on the Catholic conception, one cannot affirm that the Manichaeans had the Eucharist. It was unthinkable for them that a material element could become an instrument of salvation, particularly the wine that their myth considers as the gall of demons (XVI 31; De moribus Il 16,44; De haeres. 46,11). However, sometimes, without using the term itself, the sources express themselves in such a way that it cannot be said that it is not a Manichean Eucharist. So in Augustine and so in Manichean sources.

In his debate with the Manichean presbyter Fortunatus, Augustine says: «I have heard from you that you also frequently receive the Eucharist; But, not knowing when you received it, how could I know what you received? (C. Fortun. 3). What he claims to not know here he reveals to us in De haeres. 46,9, where he speaks of a "Eucharist" consisting of consuming flour sprinkled with human semen, and he alludes to this in two other texts (De moribus Y 18,66 and De natura boní 45). In this regard, it should be noted that in the text of De moribis Augustine speaks of "suspicion"; That is to say, rather than relating real facts, he draws consequences that he believes are logically derived from the Manichean system: "And since such seeds (=human semen) cannot be presented to you by your "listeners" so that you can purify them, who will not come to suspect that you yourself carry out these secret purifications and that you hide such infamous actions from them so that they do not abandon you? And if you don't do it - I hope that's the case - don't you see what suspicions your imagination gives free rein to? He returns to the same point in De natura boni, linking such practices with what they read in Manés's book El Tesoro: "These unfortunate people do not realize that it is not without reason that what they try in vain to deny is attributed to them, as long as they do not condemn his books and stop being Manichaeans" (ibid.).

Augustine, who provides names of people who attested to it, also points out that the Manichaeans denied everything, attributing them to others who usurped their name (De haeres. 46,9). Taking into account that this work was written at the end of his life, in the year 428-429, we must accept that Augustine took this conviction with him, certainly interested. Since he had heard them speak of a "Eucharist", it was easy for him to take as true what, apparently, was no more than a slander. (The discussion on the historicity of the Augustinian data, also present in other sources, can be seen in E. Décrer, L'Afrique 1 132,139). The Manichaeans spoke, yes, of a "Eucharist", but it was another Eucharist.

Going from less to more, in the Manichean sources we find mentions of the "Table" (Manichean Homilies, 16,21; 28,11), which can become "Table of piety" (CMC 35,7) or "Divine Table" (Prayer and Penitential Directory for the Manichaeans, ed. by W. Henning [cf. A. BOHLIG,
806 Supplementary notes Die Gnosis Y, 196)). "Divine table" which is nothing other than the daily food that the "elect" eat and that is provided by the "listeners."
In CMC 96,20-97,10 it is reported that the earth spoke and said to Alcasai who was carrying the plow: "Why do you get your product from me?" Then
Icasai took dust from the land that had spoken to him, shed tears,

He kissed it, placed it on his chest and began to say: "This is the flesh and blood of my Lord." In the aforementioned Directory, the chosen one confesses that in the daily meal he has not thought whose flesh and blood he has drunk (A. BóntiG, Díe Gnosis YI, p.197). The Chinese Hymn Scroll (Tsur Chi: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 11, [1943], p.198; we take it from ZEP 32 [1978] p.193), it reads: «All the wonderful offerings that are received, according to E said by the Law, are restored to the original Law, dignified and solemn, clean and pure. And these are exactly the flesh and blood of Jesus. Bishop Faustus writes: "From the religious point of view, we think in a similar way with reference to everything that exists and you with respect to the bread and the chalice" (XX 2). Finally, Dr. Félix writes: "If there is nothing contrary to God, what purpose does the Eucharist have?" (C. Fel. 1 19).

From all these data it can be deduced that, perhaps due to missionary considerations, the Manichaeans had no qualms about designating their daily food as "Flesh and Blood of Jesus" to accentuate the connection with the Holy Supper of Catholics (cf. E. Ros£, Die manicháische Christologie, p.99). We have already indicated (cf. complementary note 8) that the food of the Manichaeans not only had the function of keeping the "elect" alive, but also and above all that of obtaining the release of the particles of light imprisoned in the matter of the food they ate. In short, this "Eucharist" cannot be disconnected from the doctrine on lesus patibilis (cf. complementary note 7). The chosen one mystically communes with the lesus patibilis and contributes to his liberation. Cf. also H.C. PuecH, Le manicheisme, p.184, n. 367.
B1] The historical Jesus (XX 11).—It is the second aspect of Manichean Christology to which Augustine refers (XX 11; cf. complementary note 7).

The Manichaeans, who considered themselves Christians, could not ignore the historical Jesus they saw in Palestine. But their conception of it was substantially different from the Catholic one. The statement is valid in two aspects: in terms of its function and in terms of its reality itself.

Regarding his function, Jesus is one of the prophets of truth, next to Buddha, Zarathustra and others (cf. supplementary note 28), without a doubt the most important, but he is not so in the same way as the others. «Jesus is the cosmic Son of God (Keph. 1,12,19-20); the disciple's question and Manes' response in Keph. 112,267,18-268,18 presuppose the identity between the cosmic Jesus, Jesus Splendor and the historical Jesus» (N.A. PeDERsSEN, Early, p.169). He is the only one to whom, as we will see, all reality is denied Bumanas otherwise it would imply that God allowed himself to be contaminated by the kingdom of darkness. Through him the original revelation communicated to Adam reached the West; As for the content, it did not provide any novelty, limiting itself to transmitting it. In addition to not being "original", it is not presented as the definitive revealer. He himself warned that it would not be the last, announcing a Paraclete, whom the Manichaeans identify with Manes (cf. supplementary note 18), who would introduce the complete truth. On the one hand, its activity was not universal, but

Geographically it was limited to the west, while that of Manés spread to the east and west. On the other hand, he did not leave his doctrine in writing, which favored the spread of the error. Indeed, his teachings were
Supplementary notes 807 altered or totally falsified through numerous interpolations! carried out by Judaizing elements (cf. supplementary note 19).

As for their being, the Manichaeans do not accept their human condition as real. The body that the Jews, his contemporaries, saw was nothing but apparent. Augustine constantly refers to this Docetism. The ultimate foundation is dogmatic, as we already indicated: Jesus, the Son of God, could not take on a human body that has its origins in the devil. To this dogmatic foundation they add the biblical proof, namely, Phil 2,57: Christ took the form (appearance) of a man (Keph. 1,12,24-26; C. Fortun. 7).

Consequently, they completely reject several facts about the life of Jesus. Faust writes: «To be born from a woman is a clumsy act; being circumcised like the Jews is equivalent to a Gentile sacrifice; being baptized, a humiliating act; to be led by the devil into the desert and to be tempted by him, the most miserable thing” (XXX 7; cf, also HI 1; XIV 1; XX 11; XXIN 2; XXVI 1; XXIX 1.3; XXX 6). Consequently, they also reject the adoration of the magi, since the story would imply submission to the stars (II 5).

The treatment they give to the passion and death of the Lord is different. Here they do not simply deny the facts but speak of fiction or simulation: he simulated the appearance of flesh, he simulated death on a cross, the wounds of the passion and even the scars of the resurrection (V 5; XVI 11; cf. also VI 9; XV 11; XXIX 3). At the same time, they maintain the language of the crucifixion: "We believe..., in addition to his mystical crucifixion, by which the wounds of his passion are shown to our soul (XXXII 7; cf. also XX 11; XXXU 7; XIV 1). Needless to say, when referring to Christ, there is no room for an authentic crucifixion, starting from a total decerism. It has a figurative meaning, included in the adjective "mystical", which is related to another aspect of the figure of Jesus, the lesus patíbilis (cf. complementary note 7). The historical Jesus becomes for the Manichaeans a symbol of that lesus patibilis or the cross of light (Exarr. in ps. 140,12). The simulated passion of the historical Jesus well expresses the sufferings of the other figure of Jesus.

But the Manichean sources do not only mention this mystical crucifixion. They also allude to a crucifixion in the proper sense. According to them, there was indeed a crucifixion, but it was not of Jesus, but of another in his place. As it seems to be deduced from the Book of the Mysteries of Manes (A. Apam, Texte, 2) the one crucified on Golgotha ​​was not Jesus, but the Messiah, it is understood that of the Jews. This is confirmed by fragment M 28, which distinguishes the Son of God from the Son of Mary, accusing "Christians" of worshiping the second for the first. Mary's son would be the Messiah awaited by the Jews whom they themselves crucified. The text of the Letter of the Foundation must be understood along the same lines, according to which the enemy who hoped to have crucified the Savior, father of the just, was himself crucified (EvoDIo, De fide 28).

Seven Chapters 127-128 refer to the same distinction between the Son of Mary and the Savior (which is followed by the Great Greek formula of abjuration): one was the one who was born of Mary and was immersed in the Jordan to

be baptized (4,107-120), and another the one who came out of the waters [cf. XXIII 2] "whom they call Jesus and Shining", appearing in human form (4.127130). Likewise, the first person was crucified, while Jesus stood at a distance laughing at the deception (5,134-135; cf. S.C.N. Liu, An Early Byzantine Formula, p.180-182.206-208).

Another tradition presupposes that the crucified person was the ghostly body of Jesus. On the cross, he left his ghostly body in a kind of personal resurrection or ascension that is not subject to death (Psalm
808 Additional notes

196,29.20-28). Thus the attempt to kill Jesus becomes a defeat in that death only finds the ghostly body that is supernatural in nature and is not subject to death. In both cases Jesus defeats death and evil, although by making them believe that they have crucified him. It is a victory of light over darkness.

The other facts of the life of Jesus have no difficulty in admitting, both the miracles and, above all, the preaching. Faustus continues writing: "We believe... both his salutary precepts and his parables which, by presenting above all the distinction of the two natures, there is no doubt that they are his" (XXXII 7). With these words, Faustus alludes to something that appears well documented both in his writing and in Augustine's reply: they accept everything contained in the gospels, as long as it is in accordance with the backbone of their dogmatic system, that is, the dualism of natures. Such is the criterion that will serve to admit something as authentically coming from the mouth of Jesus or not. Whatever, in your opinion, does not fit, has been falsified or interpolated, and therefore should not be accepted. See: E, RosE, Die manicbiische Cbristologie, p.117-131 and N.A. PEDERSEN, Early, cited above.

[521 The Cosric Jesus (XX 11).—It is the third aspect of Manichaean Christology to which Augustine explicitly alludes (cf. complementary note 7), although without using either the cosmic adjective or the noun Jesus. If he talks about Christ and not Jesus, it must be attributed to imprecision of language. The bishop of Hippo puts it in relation to the two largest stars in the firmament; in fact he speaks of the Christ who “spreads across the sun and the moon” (XX 11). But such a relationship is not his, since it arises in his pen within the response to Faustus' presentation of the Manichean Trinity. In it, the second place is occupied by the Son who subsists in this derived and visible light; Son who is double, with reference to 1 Cor 1:24: Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God, and who believe that as Power he dwells in the sun and as Wisdom he waves in the moon (XX 2). It is therefore androgynous, in that Power (virtus) refers to its masculine aspect and Wisdom (sapientia) to its feminine aspect, collecting Gnostic conceptions (E.RosE, Die manicháische Christologie, p.166). Augustine's own is the statement that it "extends" through the sun and the moon, meaning that it expands and contracts to the extent that these stars do, particularly the moon in its various phases. Faust limits himself to saying that he has his home in them, thanks to their purity (cf. complementary note 15). From them, there it exercises its liberating function, at a cosmic level, of the divine light, as it sets in motion the great mechanism designed for this purpose (cf. complementary note 15). Leave in your role as active redeemer. C£. E. RosE, Die manicháische Christologie, p.154-176.

[531 The Manichaeans and Saint Paul (XXIL 55).—Within the vigorous exhortation that the Manichean listener Secundino addresses to Augustine is this recommendation: "Revive Paul in our times" (Epist. Secund. 5). Such words denote the esteem that the Manichaeans had for the Apostle. This was such among the African Manichaeans that someone has been able to write that "African Manichaeism is almost a Paulinist heresy" (W.H.C. FreND, The Gnostic-Manichaean Tradition in Roman North-Africa: The Journal of Ecclesiastical History 4 (1953) p.21. They denote, at the same time, that he was the model to imitate, the model of Christian life.

In line with their moral teaching, they highlight a particular aspect: that which is related to their appreciation and promotion of life in chastity. It is enough to bring here some words from Faust: «... the apostle Paul, who is known to have put unmarried women before married women in all places and times and showed it

Supplementary notes 809 also in his behavior towards the most holy Thecla” (XXX 4, with reference to the Apocryphal Acts of Paul and Thecla; cf. supplementary note 34). The Manichean bishop highlights not only the Apostle's teaching, but also his own coherence with said teaching.

Saint Paul is also the example of the Manichaean apostle. When Augustine personifies the apostolic life in him (XXII 55: "Therefore, the Apostolic Life, burdened by the fatigue of the chains, says...") his words very probably owe something to the conception of the Manichaeans in this regard (on the connection between the apostolate of Manes and Saint Paul, cf. J. RiES, Saint Paul dans la formation de Mani: J. Rius - F. DÉcreT - W.H.C. FrEND - M.G. Mara: Le epistole paoline p.17.24-26). His continuous pilgrimage, the endless and continuous persecutions that he had to face, his incessant work, his own martyrdom constituted him as an unsurpassable model, especially for the "chosen ones", lifelong missionaries like him. To the point that one of the concerns of the Manichaeans will be to try to adjust Paul's life with that of the chosen one, particularly at the conflict point of work. While Paul worked with his hands, the “elect” could not do so by virtue of the hand seal (cf. supplementary note 13). This made them see the need to exchange one job for another: the work of the "elect" is the missionary task of announcing the doctrine of salvation. Incoherent solution, without a doubt, since in Paul one did not eliminate the other (cf. F. DÉckEr, Aspects, p.138-142).

St. Paul is also one of the pillars of his anti-Catholic controversy. In his street or official disputes, the Apostle was, along with the gospel, the source from which the Catholics drank the arguments and quotes that they opposed to their adversaries. Unequivocal testimony of this are those maintained by Agustín with the priest Fortunato and with Dr. Félix. The priest repeatedly quotes the apostolic letters: four texts from Romans; one of 1 Stintios; two from Galatians; two from Ephesians and one from Philippians. The doctor, for his part, cites Romans twice, once 1 Corinthians, twice 2 Corinthians and once Galatians (cf. F. DÉcRET, Aspects, p.168.172).

In written controversy, Paul is also a sure point of reference. Pablo provides reasons. Equally unequivocal testimony is the work at hand, Contra Faustum. The Maniguean bishop explicitly or implicitly alludes to numerous passages, some of them repeatedly, from the writings that bear the name of the Apostle: eight from Romans, five from 1 Corinthians, three from 2 Corinthians, five from Galatians, three from Ephesians, one from Philippians, three from Colossians, three from 1 Timothy, 2 Titus and one from Hebrews (cf. F. DÉcrrT, Aspects, p.168-172). Although his position regarding them is not always the same, since in some cases, he will cite them to reject them as interpolated (cf. complementary note 19), they always remain as testimony of a deep knowledge of such writings, the result of assiduous reading. On the other hand, Adeimantus, in his desire to disqualify the Old Testament, showing it to be opposed to the New, is more sparing in his recourse to the Apostle. However, he still quotes 1 Corinthians three times, 1 Timothy twice, Romans, Galatians and Colossians once.
